sections.title: Sets before formulas
sections.text: The intersection A∩B contains inputs allowed by both restrictions; the union A∪B allows either. The interval [a,b) includes a and excludes b. A function assigns exactly one output to every member of its domain. Its codomain is the declared target set; its range consists of outputs actually attained.

sections.title: Derive the domain
sections.text: For f(x)=√(x−1)/(x−2), the root requires x≥1 and the denominator requires x≠2. Intersecting gives [1,2)∪(2,∞). Declaring only [3,4] as the domain defines a different, restricted function. A circle as a relation fails the function test where one input has two output heights.

exercise.prompt: Let $f:[-2,2]\to\mathbb R$ be $f(x)=x^2$. Identify domain, codomain and range. Can the same rule define a function into $[1,4]$?
exercise.hint: Check the output at x=0; then show that every value in your proposed range is attained.
exercise.solution: The domain is [−2,2], codomain ℝ, and range [0,4]. Every y in [0,4] is attained at x=√y. The proposed codomain [1,4] fails because f(0)=0 lies outside it.
rubric: Separate declared inputs from allowed outputs.
Prove both inclusion and attainment for the range.
Use an explicit input to refute the proposed codomain.

sections.title: Classify with the domain
sections.text: Even means f(−x)=f(x), odd means f(−x)=−f(x), and either requires a domain symmetric about zero. Restricting x² to [0,2] removes evenness under this convention. Increasing means x₁<x₂ implies f(x₁)≤f(x₂); strict increase replaces ≤ with <. The function x³ is strictly increasing although its derivative vanishes at zero.

sections.title: Families and junctions
sections.text: Polynomials have real natural domains; rational functions exclude denominator zeros. Exponentials are positive, logarithms require positive inputs, and trigonometric domains depend on the function: tan excludes π/2+kπ. For a piecewise function, inspect each formula on its assigned interval and compare both limiting heights with the actual junction value. The identity |x|=−x for x<0 and x for x≥0 makes its corner explicit.

exercise.prompt: Is $f(x)=x^3$ on $[-1,2]$ odd, strictly increasing, both, or neither?
exercise.hint: Test domain symmetry independently of the algebraic identity.
exercise.solution: It is strictly increasing, since x₁³<x₂³ whenever x₁<x₂. It is not odd under the symmetric-domain convention: 2 belongs to the domain but −2 does not.
rubric: Distinguish strict monotonicity from a derivative being everywhere positive.

sections.title: Track a point
sections.text: For g(x)=a f(b(x−h))+k with b≠0, a point (u,f(u)) maps to (h+u/b,k+a f(u)). A negative b reflects the input direction; a negative a reflects output heights. If b=0 and f(0) exists, g is constant a f(0)+k; the inverse point mapping is unavailable.

sections.title: Order changes the domain
sections.text: For f(x)=√x and g(x)=x−1, f∘g has domain [1,∞) and value √(x−1). The reverse composition g∘f has domain [0,∞) and value √x−1. In each case require the inner input to exist and the inner output to belong to the outer domain.

exercise.prompt: If $(2,3)$ lies on f, where does it move under $g(x)=-2 f(-3(x-1))+4$?
exercise.hint: Solve −3(x−1)=2 before changing the output.
exercise.solution: The input is x=1−2/3=1/3; the output is −2·3+4=−2. The new point is (1/3,−2).
rubric: Apply output scaling and translation in order.

sections.title: Four different failures
sections.text: A removable hole has equal finite one-sided limits but no matching point value. A jump has unequal one-sided limits. The function 1/x² tends to +∞ at zero, which is not a finite limit. The bounded function sin(1/x) oscillates: inputs approaching zero can give outputs 1 or −1.

sections.title: A rate with units
sections.text: If position is s(t)=t² metres with t in seconds, average velocity over [2,2+h] is ((2+h)²−4)/h=4+h metres per second. As h tends to zero from either side, velocity tends to 4 m/s. The h=0 quotient is undefined; its limit supplies the instantaneous rate.

exercise.prompt: For $f(x)=x+1$ when $x\ne 1$ and $f(1)=7$, find the limit at 1. Which point value makes f continuous?
exercise.hint: The punctured neighborhood contains no information about f(1).
exercise.solution: Both one-sided limits are 2. Setting f(1)=2 restores continuity. Changing only f(1) cannot repair a jump with unequal one-sided limits.
rubric: Explain why one-point repair needs a pre-existing finite limit.

sections.title: Quantifiers and signs
sections.text: A right-hand limit of +∞ at a means: for each M>0 there exists δ>0 such that 0<x−a<δ implies f(x)>M. Replace f(x)>M by f(x)<−M for −∞. For 1/x, the right limit at zero is +∞ and the left limit is −∞; for 1/x² both are +∞.

sections.title: Unbounded is weaker
sections.text: A denominator zero can be removable: (x²−1)/(x−1) has limit 2 at 1. The function sin(1/x)/x is unbounded near zero but does not tend to either infinity: along x=1/(nπ) its value is zero. A graph clipped at a finite height cannot certify an infinite limit.

exercise.prompt: Prove that $1/x^2$ tends to $+\infty$ as $x\to 0$.
exercise.hint: Given M, choose δ so that δ²=1/M.
exercise.solution: For M>0 choose δ=1/√M. If 0<|x|<δ, then x²<1/M, hence 1/x²>M. This works on both sides.

sections.title: Eligibility before arithmetic
sections.text: The sum and product laws require the component finite limits to exist; the quotient law additionally requires a nonzero denominator limit. A quotient 0/0 calls for another argument. Cancellation is valid in a punctured neighborhood even if the original expression is undefined at the target.

sections.title: Build an estimate
sections.text: Since |sin(1/x)|≤1, |x sin(1/x)|≤|x|. Given ε>0, taking δ=ε bounds the output error for every nonzero |x|<δ. This establishes a limit without requiring the oscillating factor to have one.

exercise.prompt: Find $\lim_{x\to0}x^2\cos(1/x)$, justifying the estimate.
exercise.hint: Bound the absolute value by a non-oscillating function.
exercise.solution: The absolute value is at most x². For ε>0 use δ=√ε. Then 0<|x|<δ implies |x²cos(1/x)|<ε, so the limit is zero.
rubric: Use a bound valid for every nearby input.
Do not assign a limit to cos(1/x).

sections.title: The order matters
sections.text: The statement is: for every ε>0 there exists δ>0 such that every allowed x with 0<|x−a|<δ satisfies |f(x)−L|<ε. The chosen δ may depend on ε and a, but not on the particular x. Its negation has some ε₀>0 for which every δ>0 admits a violating input.

sections.title: A nonlinear estimate
sections.text: To prove x²→4 as x→2, factor |x²−4|=|x−2||x+2|. First require |x−2|<1, giving |x+2|<5. Then choose δ=min(1,ε/5). The same δ enforces both the local bound and the requested output tolerance.

exercise.prompt: Give a valid $\delta$ for proving $3x+2\to 5$ as $x\to 1$, and explain why it works.
exercise.hint: Express output error as a multiple of input error.
exercise.solution: Since |(3x+2)−5|=3|x−1|, choose δ=ε/3. Every 0<|x−1|<δ gives output error less than ε.
rubric: State that ε is arbitrary and positive.

sections.title: Continuity depends on the domain
sections.text: At an endpoint of an interval, continuity is tested through the domain, so only the available side matters. At an interior point, existence of the finite limit and equality to the point value are both required.

sections.title: Existence is not uniqueness
sections.text: For f(x)=x³−x−1, f(1)=−1 and f(2)=5. Polynomial continuity and the intermediate value theorem give a zero in (1,2). This theorem alone does not count zeros. Bisection repeatedly retains an interval whose endpoint values bracket zero; discontinuity would invalidate its existence guarantee.

exercise.prompt: Why does a sign change in $f(x)=1/x$ between −1 and 1 not guarantee a zero?
exercise.hint: Which hypothesis fails on the closed interval?
exercise.solution: The function is not defined or continuous at zero, so IVT cannot be applied on [−1,1]. Indeed 1/x is never zero on its domain.
rubric: Check the entire interval, not just its endpoints.
Separate a failed theorem application from the truth of its conclusion.

sections.title: Derive before substituting
sections.text: For f(x)=x², the secant quotient at a is ((a+h)²−a²)/h=2a+h for h≠0. The derivative is the limit 2a. On the graph, the secant line uses two distinct points; the tangent is the limiting line, not a zero-length secant.

sections.title: Two derivative functions
sections.text: A derivative at a is a number. The derivative function f′ assigns that number to every point where the limit exists. If f measures metres and x seconds, f′ measures metres per second; a second derivative measures metres per second squared.

exercise.prompt: Use the definition to differentiate $f(x)=1/x$ at $a\ne 0$.
exercise.hint: Combine the fractions before cancelling h; keep a+h nonzero.
exercise.solution: The quotient is (1/(a+h)−1/a)/h=−1/(a(a+h)). As h→0 this tends to −1/a². Choose a neighborhood with |h|<|a|/2 to keep denominators nonzero.
rubric: Show the algebraic cancellation only for h≠0.
State a≠0 and control nearby denominators.

sections.title: Three obstructions
sections.text: For |x| at zero, the difference quotient is −1 from the left and 1 from the right: a corner. For x^(1/3), its quotient at zero is |h|^(−2/3), which has no finite limit: a vertical tangent does not supply a finite derivative. A discontinuity also prevents differentiability.

sections.title: Why differentiability implies continuity
sections.text: Write f(a+h)−f(a)=h·((f(a+h)−f(a))/h). If the quotient has a finite limit, multiplying by h→0 gives an increment tending to zero. The converse fails, as |x| demonstrates.

exercise.prompt: Is $f(x)=|x-2|$ differentiable at 2? State the one-sided quotients.
exercise.hint: Set x=2+h.
exercise.solution: The quotient |h|/h equals −1 for h<0 and 1 for h>0. It has no two-sided limit, although f is continuous at 2.

sections.title: Choose the outer operation
sections.text: A product differentiates as f′g+fg′; a quotient as (f′g−fg′)/g² where g≠0. In radians, (sin x)′=cos x and (cos x)′=−sin x. The expression x sin x is a product, so its derivative is sin x+x cos x.

sections.title: A quotient worked through
sections.text: For q(x)=sin x/x on x≠0, numerator derivative is cos x and denominator derivative is 1. Thus q′(x)=(x cos x−sin x)/x². The derivative formula has the same excluded zero; any extension at zero must be defined and differentiated separately.

exercise.prompt: Differentiate $(x^2+1)/(x-1)$ and state its domain.
exercise.hint: Use the quotient rule with the numerator derivative 2x.
exercise.solution: For x≠1, the derivative is [2x(x−1)−(x²+1)]/(x−1)²=(x²−2x−1)/(x−1)².
rubric: Preserve the minus sign before the entire numerator.

sections.title: Make little-o explicit
sections.text: The notation r(h)=o(h) means r(h)/h→0. Differentiability of g at a says g(a+h)=g(a)+g′(a)h+o(h). Differentiability of f at g(a) lets its output increment be f′(g(a)) times the inner increment plus a smaller error. Combining gives derivative f′(g(a))g′(a); the argument also covers g′(a)=0.

sections.title: Layers and domains
sections.text: For y=sin(x²), the outer function is sin and the inner is x², giving y′=cos(x²)·2x. For ln(1+x²), divide the inner derivative 2x by the positive inner value 1+x². Naming layers prevents replacing cos(x²) by cos x.

exercise.prompt: Differentiate $(1+\sin x)^3$.
exercise.hint: Differentiate the cube with respect to its input, then multiply by the derivative of that input.
exercise.solution: The derivative is 3(1+sin x)² cos x, for every real x.
rubric: Keep the full inner expression in the squared factor.

sections.title: Differentiate an identity on a branch
sections.text: From x²+y²=25, assuming a differentiable local branch y(x), differentiate to get 2x+2yy′=0. Where y≠0, y′=−x/y. At (3,4) the tangent slope is −3/4. At y=0 this formula cannot solve for y′; a different local graph may be needed.

sections.title: Rates carry units
sections.text: For a spherical balloon V=(4π/3)r³, differentiation in time gives dV/dt=4πr² dr/dt. If dV/dt=12π cm³/s at r=3 cm, then dr/dt=1/3 cm/s. Substitute the instantaneous radius after differentiating, since it varies in time.

exercise.prompt: A 5 m ladder has foot distance x and height y with $x^2+y^2=25$. At $x=3$ m its foot moves outward at 2 m/s. Find $dy/dt$.
exercise.hint: Use y=4 and differentiate with respect to time.
exercise.solution: 2x dx/dt+2y dy/dt=0, so dy/dt=−(3/4)·2=−3/2 m/s. The negative sign means the top descends.

sections.title: Linear versus affine
sections.text: The derivative is the linear map h↦f′(a)h. The approximating graph x↦f(a)+f′(a)(x−a) is affine because it includes an offset. Differentiability guarantees error o(|x−a|), not a chosen finite error bound for arbitrary steps.

sections.title: Approximate with an error bound
sections.text: For √x near a=4, L(x)=2+(x−4)/4, so L(4.1)=2.025. Taylor’s theorem gives error at most M(0.1)²/2 if |f″|≤M between 4 and 4.1. Here |f″|=1/(4x^(3/2))≤1/32, so the error is at most 0.00015625. This finite bound is stronger than a bare little-o statement.

exercise.prompt: Use linearization at 0 to approximate $\sin(0.02)$. What extra information would certify an error bound?
exercise.hint: Use sin 0=0 and cos 0=1; a remainder estimate needs derivative control.
exercise.solution: The linear estimate is 0.02. Taylor’s theorem and |sin″x|≤1 give error at most (0.02)²/2=0.0002. A sharper cubic bound is possible using additional vanishing terms.
rubric: State the theorem and derivative bound for the error.

sections.title: A convention for candidates
sections.text: Here a critical point is an interior domain point where f′=0 or f′ does not exist; a stationary point has f′=0. Endpoints are checked separately. Fermat’s theorem says that a differentiable interior local extremum is stationary, not that every stationary point is an extremum.

sections.title: List, then compare
sections.text: For f(x)=x³−3x on [−2,2], f′=3x²−3 vanishes at ±1. Evaluate endpoints and stationary points: f(−2)=−2, f(−1)=2, f(1)=−2, f(2)=2. The global minimum is −2 at −2 and 1; the maximum is 2 at −1 and 2. Compactness and continuity ensure attainment.

exercise.prompt: Why does $f(x)=x$ on $[0,1]$ have a maximum even though $f'$ never vanishes?
exercise.hint: Is the maximum an interior point?
exercise.solution: The maximum is f(1)=1 at an endpoint. Fermat’s necessary condition applies only to differentiable interior extrema, so there is no contradiction.
rubric: Do not infer no extrema from no stationary points.

sections.title: Rolle’s theorem supplies the bridge
sections.text: If f is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and f(a)=f(b), extrema are attained. If f is constant, any interior point has derivative zero. Otherwise a value differs from the common endpoint value, so a maximum or minimum occurs inside; Fermat gives derivative zero there.

sections.title: Subtract the secant
sections.text: Set g(x)=f(x)−f(a)−m(x−a), where m=(f(b)−f(a))/(b−a). Then g(a)=g(b)=0. Rolle provides c with g′(c)=0, hence f′(c)=m. For f(x)=x² on [1,3], m=4 and c=2.

exercise.prompt: Why can the mean value theorem not be used for $|x|$ on $[-1,1]$?
exercise.hint: Check differentiability at the interior junction.
exercise.solution: The endpoint slope is zero, but |x| is not differentiable at zero and its derivative elsewhere is ±1. The missing differentiability hypothesis prevents the claimed conclusion.
rubric: Name the failed hypothesis and its location.
Compute the secant and available derivatives.

sections.title: Continuity is indispensable
sections.text: The derivative signs constrain nearby motion but do not fix a separately assigned point height. The example f(x)=−|x| for x≠0 with f(0)=−1 has the positive-to-negative derivative pattern and nevertheless a strict local minimum at zero.

sections.title: Zero second derivative gives no verdict
sections.text: At zero, x⁴ has a strict minimum, −x⁴ a strict maximum, and x³ neither, although all three have first and second derivatives zero there. Check derivative signs or the original value comparison. An inflection point requires a change of concavity, not merely f″=0.

exercise.prompt: Classify $x^4$ at zero without using an inconclusive second-derivative test.
exercise.hint: Compare f(x) with f(0) for nonzero x.
exercise.solution: For x≠0, x⁴>0=f(0), so zero is a strict global and local minimum. Equivalently f′=4x³ changes from negative to positive.
rubric: Identify why the second-derivative test is inconclusive.
Supply a direct inequality or valid sign test.

sections.title: Separate the two tails
sections.text: For rational functions, divide by the highest denominator power separately as x→+∞ and x→−∞. For √(x²+1)/x, factoring produces |x|/x times √(1+1/x²), giving limits 1 and −1. Replacing √(x²) by x would lose the negative tail.

sections.title: A sketch is an assembled argument
sections.text: For f(x)=x+1/x, domain excludes zero. Its slant asymptote is y=x because f(x)−x→0 at both infinities. Derivative 1−1/x² is positive for |x|>1 and negative for 0<|x|<1; stationary points are −1 and 1. Add the separate vertical behavior at zero before drawing connected pieces.

exercise.prompt: Find the slant asymptote of $(x^2+1)/(x-1)$.
exercise.hint: Perform polynomial division.
exercise.solution: (x²+1)/(x−1)=x+1+2/(x−1). The remainder tends to zero at either infinity, so y=x+1 is the slant asymptote; x=1 remains excluded.

sections.title: Model the feasible set
sections.text: A rectangle with perimeter 20 has y=10−x and area A=x(10−x). Positive side lengths require 0<x<10; including degenerate rectangles closes the set to [0,10]. Differentiate A to get 10−2x, whose zero is x=5. Then y=5 and A=25.

sections.title: Justify a global answer
sections.text: The identity A=25−(x−5)² proves A≤25 throughout the feasible set. This proves global optimality directly, whereas a positive-to-negative sign change by itself describes local behavior. Check units: perimeter in metres gives area in square metres.

exercise.prompt: Find the largest area rectangle with perimeter $P>0$.
exercise.hint: Eliminate one side and complete the square.
exercise.solution: With y=P/2−x, A=x(P/2−x)=P²/16−(x−P/4)². Its maximum P²/16 occurs at x=y=P/4, within the positive feasible interval.
rubric: State positivity and the feasible interval.

sections.title: Derive the update
sections.text: The tangent at xₙ has equation y=f(xₙ)+f′(xₙ)(x−xₙ). Setting y=0 gives xₙ₊₁=xₙ−f(xₙ)/f′(xₙ), provided the derivative is nonzero. It finds a tangent intercept, not an exact root of the original curve.

sections.title: Failure deserves an example
sections.text: For f(x)=x³−2x+2, starting at 0 gives 1 and starting at 1 gives 0, so Newton cycles. For x²−2, starting at zero is undefined because f′(0)=0. A small step alone is not proof of a root; check the residual and the domain, and use a bracket when available.

exercise.prompt: Perform two Newton steps for $x^2-2$ from $x_0=1$.
exercise.hint: Use xₙ₊₁=(xₙ+2/xₙ)/2.
exercise.solution: x₁=3/2 and x₂=17/12. The residual at the second iterate is (17/12)²−2=1/144; it is an approximation, not an exact root.

sections.title: Why the constant is the only freedom
sections.text: If F′=G′ on an interval, then (F−G)′=0. Applying MVT between any two points gives equal values of F−G. Thus F−G is constant on that interval. On a disconnected domain the constants may differ between components.

sections.title: Use initial data
sections.text: If velocity is v(t)=3t²−2 and s(0)=5, integrating gives s(t)=t³−2t+C. The initial value sets C=5. Differentiation recovers the velocity and checks the answer; the constant carries position units.

exercise.prompt: Find every antiderivative of $1/x$ on $\mathbb R$ excluding zero.
exercise.hint: Treat the negative and positive intervals separately.
exercise.solution: The answer is ln|x|+C₋ for x<0 and ln|x|+C₊ for x>0, with independent constants. No interval in this domain connects the two sides.
rubric: Use ln|x|, not ln x on negative inputs.
Allow separate constants on disconnected components.

sections.title: Existence precedes the derivative
sections.text: A continuous strictly monotone function on an interval has an inverse on its range. A sufficient local differentiability theorem assumes f is continuously differentiable near a and f′(a)≠0; then its local inverse is differentiable near f(a). Only after this theorem may differentiating f(f⁻¹(y))=y establish (f⁻¹)′(y)=1/f′(f⁻¹(y)).

sections.title: Zero derivative is a warning
sections.text: The inverse of x³ is the cube root. Although x³ is one-to-one, its derivative at zero vanishes and the inverse has no finite derivative there. For x², choose a branch such as [0,∞) before naming √x as its inverse.

exercise.prompt: For $f(x)=x^3+x$, find the derivative of its inverse at $y=2$.
exercise.hint: Find the input mapped to 2, then evaluate f′ there.
exercise.solution: f(1)=2 and f′(1)=3+1=4, so (f⁻¹)′(2)=1/4. Since f′=3x²+1>0, the inverse is well-defined and differentiable.
rubric: Evaluate at the inverse input, not at y directly.

sections.title: A definition must have a foundation
sections.text: One rigorous route defines ln x as the integral from 1 to x of 1/t for x>0, then uses the fundamental theorem to obtain derivative 1/x. Its inverse is exp; the inverse derivative theorem yields exp′=exp. If integration has not been developed yet, these facts are imported theorems.

sections.title: Logarithmic differentiation
sections.text: For y=xˣ on x>0, take ln y=x ln x. Differentiate to obtain y′/y=ln x+1, hence y′=xˣ(ln x+1). The positive domain permits logarithms; this argument does not define a real differentiable xˣ on all negative inputs.

exercise.prompt: Differentiate $\ln(x^2-1)$ over its real domain.
exercise.hint: First require x²−1>0.
exercise.solution: The domain is (−∞,−1)∪(1,∞). The derivative is 2x/(x²−1) on that domain.

sections.title: State a usable version
sections.text: For a 0/0 quotient near a, assume f,g are differentiable on a punctured one-sided interval, g and g′ are nonzero there, both f and g tend to zero, and f′/g′ tends to L (finite or infinite). Then f/g tends to L. An infinity/infinity version has its own hypotheses. The justification imports Cauchy’s mean value theorem, a two-function extension of MVT.

sections.title: Normalize before applying
sections.text: A product x ln x as x→0+ is not itself a quotient. Rewrite it as ln x/(1/x), an infinity/infinity form. Differentiating numerator and denominator gives (1/x)/(−1/x²)=−x→0. By contrast, differentiating numerator and denominator of (x+1)/x near zero without checking form would incorrectly discard its infinite behavior.

exercise.prompt: Find $\lim_{x\to0}(e^x-1-x)/x^2$, checking the form at each step.
exercise.hint: The first derivative quotient is (eˣ−1)/(2x).
exercise.solution: Initially both numerator and denominator tend to zero. After one application they still do. The second derivative quotient is eˣ/2→1/2. Derivatives of the denominators are nonzero on each punctured side, so the limit is 1/2.
rubric: Use the rule on each side and match the results.

sections.title: An indefinite integral is a family
sections.text: The notation ∫f(x)dx denotes antiderivatives F(x)+C on an interval. It is not a signed area with unspecified endpoints. Differentiate a candidate to verify it, and handle disconnected domains separately.

sections.title: Reverse a chain rule carefully
sections.text: For ∫2x cos(x²)dx, notice that 2x is the derivative of the inner x². The answer is sin(x²)+C. Omitting 2x would produce a different problem; there is no general rule integrating a composition by simply integrating the outer function.

exercise.prompt: Find $\int(3x^2-4x+2)\,dx$ and verify it.
exercise.hint: Integrate each power, then differentiate.
exercise.solution: x³−2x²+2x+C differentiates to 3x²−4x+2. Every antiderivative on ℝ differs by one constant.
rubric: Use differentiation as an independent check.

sections.title: A partition is more than equal bars
sections.text: Partition [a,b] into subintervals, choose a tag in each, and sum f(tag) times width. Riemann integrability means all such sums approach one number as the largest width tends to zero, independently of tags. Continuous functions on a closed interval are integrable; this result uses uniform continuity.

sections.title: Signed accumulation
sections.text: For f(x)=x on [−1,1], negative left-hand contributions cancel positive right-hand contributions, giving integral zero. The geometric area is instead ∫|x|dx=1. Increasing equal bars supplies evidence but is not the definition’s all-partition proof.

exercise.prompt: Compute right-endpoint sums for x on $[0,1]$ and their limit.
exercise.hint: Use width 1/n and Σk=n(n+1)/2.
exercise.solution: The sum is Σ(k/n)(1/n)=(n+1)/(2n), tending to 1/2. Continuity independently ensures this limit equals the Riemann integral.
rubric: Distinguish one sequence of sums from the full integrability theorem.

sections.title: Average height
sections.text: On [a,b] with a<b, the integral average is (b−a)⁻¹∫f. It is the constant height producing the same signed accumulation. For a continuous function, an integral mean-value theorem ensures some c has f(c) equal to that average.

sections.title: Attainment needs care
sections.text: For f=x² on [0,2], the integral is 8/3 and average 4/3, attained at c=2/√3. A discontinuous function taking only values 0 and 1 can have average 1/2 without ever taking that value.

exercise.prompt: Find the average of $2x+1$ on $[1,3]$ and where it is attained.
exercise.hint: Divide the integral by interval length 2.
exercise.solution: The integral [x²+x]₁³ is 10, so the average is 5. Solve 2c+1=5 to get c=2.
rubric: Divide by length, not the upper endpoint.
Separate the average from the point attaining it.

sections.title: Two directions, two jobs
sections.text: If f is continuous and A(x)=$\int_a^x f(t)\,dt$, then A′(x)=f(x). If F′=f and f is continuous on [a,b], then $\int_a^b f$=F(b)−F(a). The first constructs an antiderivative; the second evaluates accumulation using one.

sections.title: Moving bounds
sections.text: For H(x)=$\int_x^{x^2}\sin t\,dt$, write A(x²)−A(x). Chain rule gives H′(x)=2x sin(x²)−sin x. The symbol t is a dummy variable; the moving endpoint x² creates its own derivative factor.

exercise.prompt: Differentiate $\int_0^{x^3}e^{t^2}\,dt$.
exercise.hint: Use FTC at the endpoint, then multiply by its derivative.
exercise.solution: The derivative is 3x² e^(x⁶). No elementary antiderivative of e^(t²) is needed.
rubric: Substitute the endpoint into the integrand.

sections.title: Transform the whole integral
sections.text: For $\int_0^1 2xe^{x^2}\,dx$, choose u=x² and du=2x dx. Bounds become 0 and 1, yielding $\int_0^1e^u\,du$=e−1. In an indefinite integral substitute back; in a definite integral either transform bounds or return to the original variable before evaluating.

sections.title: Why the rule holds
sections.text: If F′=f, then (F(g(x)))′=f(g(x))g′(x). FTC therefore gives the substitution formula when the differentiability and continuity assumptions hold. Monotonicity simplifies interpretation of transformed regions, but the signed one-variable identity with g′ can also cover paths that reverse direction.

exercise.prompt: Evaluate $\int_0^2x\sqrt{1+x^2}\,dx$.
exercise.hint: Use u=1+x²; the extra factor is du/2.
exercise.solution: The bounds become 1 and 5. The integral is (1/2)$\int_1^5u^{1/2}\,du$=(5√5−1)/3.

sections.title: Every bad endpoint gets a limit
sections.text: For $\int_1^\infty x^{-2}\,dx$, define lim R→∞ $\int_1^R x^{-2}\,dx$=lim(1−1/R)=1. For an interior singularity c, split the interval at c and require both one-sided integrals to converge separately.

sections.title: Cancellation cannot rescue divergence
sections.text: The symmetric integrals of 1/x on [−1,−ε] and [ε,1] cancel, but the negative and positive parts diverge separately. Their symmetric principal value zero is a different notion, not convergence of the improper integral.

exercise.prompt: Does $\int_0^1x^{-3/2}\,dx$ converge?
exercise.hint: Replace the lower endpoint by ε>0.
exercise.solution: The integral from ε to 1 is 2/√ε−2, tending to +∞. It diverges.
rubric: Check the sign of the antiderivative.
Distinguish divergence from a finite numerical cutoff.

sections.title: Decide the order on each piece
sections.text: Area between f and g over [a,b] is ∫|f−g|. Solve their intersections and split wherever their order changes. For x and x² on [0,1], x≥x² and the area is $\int_0^1(x-x^2)\,dx$=1/6.

sections.title: Horizontal slices are an alternative
sections.text: A horizontal slice contributes right boundary minus left boundary times dy. For x=y² and x=2−y², intersections occur at y=±1; the area is $\int_{-1}^1(2-2y^2)\,dy$=8/3. Choose an order that avoids unnecessary inverses and splitting.

exercise.prompt: Find the area between $y=x$ and $y=-x$ on $[-1,1]$.
exercise.hint: Their order switches at zero.
exercise.solution: Area is $\int_{-1}^0(-2x)\,dx$+$\int_0^1 2x\,dx$=2. The unsplit signed integral of 2x is zero and is not the area.

sections.title: A washer removes an inner disk
sections.text: Rotating y=x and y=x² for 0≤x≤1 about the x-axis gives R=x and r=x², so V=$\pi\int_0^1(x^2-x^4)\,dx$=2π/15. The slice area is π(R²−r²), not π(R−r)².

sections.title: Measure from the actual axis
sections.text: About y=−1 the same region has radii 1+x and 1+x². The volume becomes $\pi\int_0^1[(1+x)^2-(1+x^2)^2]\,dx$=7π/15. Both radii are distances from the axis, not graph heights above zero.

exercise.prompt: A region has $1\le y\le 2$ on $0\le x\le 3$. Rotate it about $y=0$; find the volume.
exercise.hint: Every slice is the same washer.
exercise.solution: V=$\int_0^3\pi(2^2-1^2)\,dx$=9π. Squaring the thickness would give only 3π and incorrectly discard part of the annulus.

sections.title: Unroll a thin shell
sections.text: A shell at radius r, height h and thickness dr has volume approximately circumference times height times thickness, 2πrh dr. Integrating gives the limit. For the region under y=x on [0,1] about the y-axis, V=$2\pi\int_0^1x^2\,dx$=2π/3.

sections.title: Choose slices relative to the axis
sections.text: Shell slices are parallel to the rotation axis; washer slices are perpendicular. Radii are nonnegative distances. If the region crosses the axis, naive shells from both sides may sweep the same volume twice; first describe the actual solid or split without overlap.

exercise.prompt: Rotate $0\le y\le 1-x$, $0\le x\le 1$, about the y-axis.
exercise.hint: Shell radius is x and height is 1−x.
exercise.solution: V=$2\pi\int_0^1x(1-x)\,dx$=π/3, agreeing with a cone of radius 1 and height 1.

sections.title: Repeated and cyclic parts
sections.text: From (uv)′=u′v+uv′, ∫u dv=uv−∫v du. Repeated parts gives ∫x²eˣdx=eˣ(x²−2x+2)+C. For I=∫eˣcos x dx, two rounds give I=eˣcos x+eˣsin x−I; solving yields I=eˣ(sin x+cos x)/2+C.

sections.title: Definite terms and choice
sections.text: For $\int_0^1xe^x\,dx$, choose u=x, dv=eˣdx. The boundary term [xeˣ]₀¹=e and the remaining integral is e−1, so the answer is 1. Choosing u=eˣ and dv=x dx creates an x²eˣ integral, increasing the polynomial degree instead of reducing it.

exercise.prompt: Evaluate $\int_0^1x^2e^x\,dx$.
exercise.hint: Use the repeated-parts antiderivative and both endpoints.
exercise.solution: The antiderivative is eˣ(x²−2x+2). Its endpoint values are e and 2, so the integral is e−2.

sections.title: Use parity to choose a substitution
sections.text: For sinᵐx cosⁿx with a positive odd sine power, reserve sin x dx and replace sin²x by 1−cos²x; then use u=cos x. With an odd cosine power, reverse the roles. If both powers are even, use half-angle identities.

sections.title: Work both branches
sections.text: ∫sin³x cos²x dx becomes −∫(1−u²)u²du=−u³/3+u⁵/5+C. For ∫cos²x dx, use cos²x=(1+cos 2x)/2, giving x/2+sin 2x/4+C.

exercise.prompt: Find $\int\sin x\cos^3x\,dx$.
exercise.hint: Reserve sin x dx and use u=cos x.
exercise.solution: The integral is −∫u³du=−cos⁴x/4+C. Differentiating restores sin x cos³x.
rubric: Carry the minus sign in du.

sections.title: Fix a branch before simplifying
sections.text: For √(a²−x²) with a>0, choose x=a sin θ and θ∈[−π/2,π/2], so cos θ≥0 and √(a²−x²)=a cos θ. Without the range restriction the root is a|cos θ|. For √(a²+x²), x=a tan θ on the same open angle interval gives a sec θ.

sections.title: Include the differential
sections.text: For ∫√(1−x²)dx, x=sin θ and dx=cos θ dθ give ∫cos²θ dθ. Substituting back gives (arcsin x+x√(1−x²))/2+C on the interior of [−1,1]. A diagram helps recover the factors but does not replace the branch choice.

exercise.prompt: Evaluate $\int_0^1\frac{dx}{\sqrt{4-x^2}}$.
exercise.hint: Use x=2 sin θ with θ from 0 to π/6.
exercise.solution: The differential and square root both contribute 2cos θ and cancel, leaving $\int_0^{\pi/6}d\theta$=π/6.

sections.title: The denominator determines the template
sections.text: First divide if numerator degree is at least denominator degree. For each repeated linear factor (x−a)ᵏ include A₁/(x−a)+…+Aₖ/(x−a)ᵏ. For an irreducible quadratic q, use a linear numerator (Bx+C)/q; repeat terms for powers of q.

sections.title: Solve coefficients explicitly
sections.text: For (x²+1)/(x(x−1)²), write A/x+B/(x−1)+C/(x−1)². Multiplying through gives x²+1=A(x−1)²+Bx(x−1)+Cx. Setting x=0 gives A=1, x=1 gives C=2, and the x² coefficient gives B=0. Integrating yields ln|x|−2/(x−1)+C₀ on each component. For (x+1)/(x²+1), split into a logarithmic derivative and an arctangent: (1/2)ln(x²+1)+arctan x.

exercise.prompt: Integrate $x^2/(x-1)$.
exercise.hint: Perform polynomial division before partial fractions.
exercise.solution: x²/(x−1)=x+1+1/(x−1). The integral is x²/2+x+ln|x−1|+C on either side of 1.
rubric: Keep the excluded point and absolute value.

sections.title: Signed errors reveal geometry
sections.text: For a convex function, chords lie above the graph, so the trapezoidal rule overestimates; midpoint underestimates when convexity holds on each panel. Error signs require hypotheses, not just a visual impression.

sections.title: Choose n from a bound
sections.text: For a twice continuously differentiable function with |f″|≤M, composite midpoint error is at most M(b−a)³/(24n²), and trapezoidal error at most M(b−a)³/(12n²). Solve the inequality for n and round up; these are certified bounds, unlike agreement between two numerical estimates.

exercise.prompt: How many trapezoids guarantee error at most 0.001 for $\int_0^1x^2\,dx$?
exercise.hint: Here M=2; require 2/(12n²)≤0.001.
exercise.solution: n²≥500/3, so n≥13 is sufficient. The bound is 1/(6·169), below 0.001.
rubric: Use an upper derivative bound on the whole interval.

sections.title: Pairs of panels
sections.text: Composite Simpson requires an even number n of equal subintervals with width h. Its weights are 1,4,2,4,…,2,4,1 and overall factor h/3. It integrates every polynomial of degree at most three exactly, although each local interpolant is quadratic.

sections.title: A fourth-derivative guarantee
sections.text: If f has a continuous fourth derivative bounded in magnitude by M, the error is at most M(b−a)⁵/(180n⁴). More panels do not make this bound applicable at a singularity; check smoothness first.

exercise.prompt: Apply Simpson with $n=2$ to $x^3$ on $[0,1]$.
exercise.hint: Use values at 0, 1/2 and 1.
exercise.solution: With h=1/2, the result is (1/6)[0+4(1/8)+1]=1/4, exactly the integral.

sections.title: The input is an index
sections.text: A sequence converges to L if for every ε>0 some integer N makes |aₙ−L|<ε for every n≥N. The tail matters: changing finitely many terms cannot change the limit. An infinite sequence does not automatically converge.

sections.title: A quantitative tail
sections.text: For aₙ=1+1/n, |aₙ−1|=1/n. Choose an integer N>1/ε; then all n≥N satisfy the required inequality. A plot of the first hundred values cannot alone establish an assertion about every later term.

exercise.prompt: Give an N ensuring $|(2+3/n)-2|<0.01$ for every $n\ge N$.
exercise.hint: Solve 3/n<0.01 with a strict inequality.
exercise.solution: Any integer N≥301 works. N=300 fails at its first term because the error equals 0.01.
rubric: Make a statement about all later indices.

sections.title: Subsequences inherit a genuine limit
sections.text: A subsequence selects indices n₁<n₂<… tending to infinity. If aₙ→L, every subsequence tends to L. Hence two subsequences with distinct limits refute convergence. For (−1)ⁿ, the even and odd subsequences tend to 1 and −1.

sections.title: Bounded does not mean convergent
sections.text: Every convergent real sequence is bounded, but (−1)ⁿ is a bounded counterexample to the converse. Bolzano–Weierstrass states that every bounded real sequence has a convergent subsequence. It does not say the whole sequence converges.

exercise.prompt: Does $a_n=(-1)^n+1/n$ converge?
exercise.hint: Separate even and odd indices.
exercise.solution: The even subsequence tends to 1 and the odd subsequence to −1. Therefore the sequence diverges while remaining bounded.
rubric: Use subsequences whose indices tend to infinity.

sections.title: Normalize polynomial growth
sections.text: For (3n²+n)/(2n²−1), divide by n² to obtain (3+1/n)/(2−1/n²), whose limit is 3/2. The denominator limit 2 is nonzero, allowing the quotient law.

sections.title: A zero denominator gives no automatic result
sections.text: The sequences 1/n and 1/n² both tend to zero, but their quotient is n and diverges. Reversing them gives 1/n→0. Equal component limits therefore do not settle an indeterminate quotient.

exercise.prompt: Find $\lim_{n\to\infty}(\sqrt{n^2+n}-n)$.
exercise.hint: Rationalize before taking limits.
exercise.solution: The expression equals n/(√(n²+n)+n)=1/(√(1+1/n)+1), tending to 1/2.
rubric: Use a valid algebraic identity for positive n.

sections.title: Prove bounds for a recurrence
sections.text: Let a₁=1 and aₙ₊₁=√(2+aₙ). If 1≤aₙ≤2, then 1≤aₙ₊₁≤2; induction bounds every term. On [1,2], √(2+x)≥x because 2+x−x²=(2−x)(x+1)≥0, so the sequence is increasing.

sections.title: Only now solve the fixed point
sections.text: An increasing bounded real sequence converges by completeness. Taking limits gives L=√(2+L), hence L=2 or −1 after squaring. The proven bounds force L=2. Solving the equation before proving convergence would produce candidates without showing that the sequence approaches any of them.

exercise.prompt: Let $b_1=3$ and $b_{n+1}=(b_n+2)/2$. Prove convergence and find the limit.
exercise.hint: Show bₙ≥2 and bₙ₊₁≤bₙ by induction.
exercise.solution: The recurrence preserves bₙ≥2, and bₙ₊₁−bₙ=(2−bₙ)/2≤0. Thus it converges. Its limit satisfies L=(L+2)/2, giving L=2; explicitly bₙ=2+2^(1−n).
rubric: Invoke convergence before passing the limit through the recurrence.

sections.title: Sum means a limit of partial sums
sections.text: For a series Σaₙ, define S_N as its first N terms. Convergence means S_N approaches a finite number, not merely aₙ→0. For Σ from n=0 of rⁿ, S_N=(1−r^(N+1))/(1−r) when r≠1; its infinite sum is 1/(1−r) only for |r|<1.

sections.title: Keep the surviving boundary terms
sections.text: For Σ from n=1 of 1/[n(n+1)], split each term into 1/n−1/(n+1). The Nth partial sum is 1−1/(N+1), tending to 1. Writing the finite cancellation first prevents informal infinity-minus-infinity errors.

exercise.prompt: Find $\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}(1/3)^n$.
exercise.hint: Identify the first term, not just the ratio.
exercise.solution: The first term is 1/9 and ratio 1/3, so the sum is (1/9)/(1−1/3)=1/6.

sections.title: Necessary is not sufficient
sections.text: If partial sums converge, then aₙ=Sₙ−Sₙ₋₁→0. Thus failure of aₙ→0 proves divergence. A zero term limit is inconclusive: Σ1/n diverges, whereas Σ1/n² converges.

sections.title: A harmonic-series proof
sections.text: Group terms from 2^(k−1)+1 to 2ᵏ. There are 2^(k−1) terms, each at least 1/2ᵏ, so each group contributes at least 1/2. Arbitrarily many groups force partial sums to grow without bound, despite individual terms tending to zero.

exercise.prompt: What does the term test say about $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n/(n+1)$ and $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}1/n^2$?
exercise.hint: Compute the term limits and distinguish a verdict from inconclusiveness.
exercise.solution: The first term limit is 1, so its series diverges. The second term limit is zero, so this test alone gives no verdict; a p-series or integral argument proves convergence.
rubric: Use the test only to rule out convergence.
Do not call the second result a proof of convergence.

sections.title: A comparison of positive tails
sections.text: If f is positive, continuous and decreasing eventually, with aₙ=f(n), then Σaₙ and ∫f share convergence behavior. Finite initial exceptions do not affect convergence. This is not an equality between sum and integral.

sections.title: Bound the remainder
sections.text: For a convergent positive decreasing series, ∫ from N+1 to ∞ of f ≤ Σ from N+1 to ∞ of aₙ ≤ ∫ from N to ∞ of f. For aₙ=1/n² this gives 1/(N+1)≤R_N≤1/N, a usable accuracy guarantee.

exercise.prompt: How large must $N$ be to guarantee remainder at most $0.001$ for $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}1/n^2$?
exercise.hint: Use the upper integral bound 1/N.
exercise.solution: N≥1000 suffices, since R_N≤1/N≤0.001. The bound is conservative and does not claim equality.
rubric: Use the upper bound for a guarantee.

sections.title: Match the inequality to the conclusion
sections.text: For nonnegative terms, aₙ≤bₙ and convergence of Σbₙ imply convergence of Σaₙ. If aₙ≥bₙ and Σbₙ diverges, Σaₙ diverges. Reversing these directions gives no conclusion.

sections.title: Limit comparison
sections.text: For positive aₙ,bₙ, if aₙ/bₙ→L with 0<L<∞, the series share behavior. For aₙ=1/(n²+n), use bₙ=1/n²: their ratio n/(n+1)→1, so the series converges. Ratio zero or infinity requires a one-sided argument rather than the same equivalence.

exercise.prompt: Decide whether $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}1/\sqrt{n^2+1}$ converges.
exercise.hint: Compare to 1/n and compute the ratio.
exercise.solution: The ratio n/√(n²+1)=1/√(1+1/n²) tends to 1. The harmonic series diverges, so this positive series diverges.
rubric: Verify a finite strictly positive ratio.

sections.title: Separate two convergence questions
sections.text: Absolute convergence means Σ|aₙ| converges and implies convergence of Σaₙ. Conditional convergence means Σaₙ converges but Σ|aₙ| diverges. The alternating harmonic series is conditional: its magnitudes decrease to zero, but their harmonic sum diverges.

sections.title: Alternating remainder
sections.text: If positive magnitudes decrease to zero, the error after N alternating terms has magnitude at most the next term and its sign matches the next term. For Σ from n=1 of (−1)^(n+1)/n, the error is at most 1/(N+1). Without eventual decrease, this bound needs another justification.

exercise.prompt: Classify $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(-1)^n/n^2$.
exercise.hint: Test the absolute-value series first.
exercise.solution: Its absolute-value series Σ1/n² converges, so the original series converges absolutely. Calling it conditional merely because signs alternate is incorrect.
rubric: Use the definition of conditional convergence.

sections.title: Different tests suit different forms
sections.text: For aₙ=xⁿ/n!, the absolute ratio is |x|/(n+1)→0, so the series converges for every fixed x. For aₙ=(n/(2n+1))ⁿ, the nth-root magnitude tends to 1/2, giving absolute convergence without expanding a complicated neighboring-term ratio.

sections.title: A limit of one is inconclusive
sections.text: Both 1/n and 1/n² have ratio and nth-root limits equal to 1, yet one series diverges and the other converges. For ratio or root limit below 1, conclude absolute convergence; above 1, terms fail to tend to zero. More general limsup forms need their own statement.

exercise.prompt: Classify $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}((3n+1)/(4n+2))^n$.
exercise.hint: The nth root removes the outer nth power.
exercise.solution: The root limit is 3/4<1, so the positive series converges absolutely.
rubric: Compare the limit with 1, not zero.

sections.title: Endpoints are separate series
sections.text: For Σ from n=1 of xⁿ/n, the ratio test gives convergence for |x|<1 and divergence for |x|>1. At x=1 it is harmonic and diverges; at x=−1 it is alternating harmonic and converges conditionally. The interval is [−1,1), not an automatically closed radius interval.

sections.title: The center shifts everything
sections.text: For Σaₙ(x−c)ⁿ, the radius measures distance from c. A radius can be zero or infinite. Partial sums are polynomials; their limit is defined only on the convergence set, and may behave differently at its boundary.

exercise.prompt: Find the interval of convergence of $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(x-2)^n/(n\,3^n)$.
exercise.hint: Use |x−2|<3, then inspect both endpoints.
exercise.solution: The radius is 3 about 2. At x=−1 the series is alternating harmonic and converges; at x=5 it is harmonic and diverges. The interval is [−1,5).
rubric: Shift the radius interval around the correct center.

sections.title: Operate inside the radius
sections.text: A power series may be differentiated or integrated term by term inside its radius, and the new series has the same radius. Endpoint convergence can change. The theorem relies on uniform control on each smaller closed interval and is imported here, rather than proved by formal symbol manipulation.

sections.title: Derive a logarithmic series
sections.text: Integrating Σ from n=0 of xⁿ=1/(1−x) from 0 to x gives Σ from n=1 of xⁿ/n=−ln(1−x) for |x|<1. The integration constant is fixed by the zero value at x=0. At x=−1 an additional endpoint argument is needed; interior validity alone does not prove it.

exercise.prompt: Differentiate $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}x^n/n$ inside its radius. What happens at $x=-1$?
exercise.hint: The differentiated coefficients lose the factor 1/n.
exercise.solution: The derivative series is Σ from n=1 of x^(n−1)=1/(1−x) for |x|<1. At x=−1 its terms alternate ±1 and do not tend to zero, so it diverges although the original series converges there.
rubric: State the open interval of termwise validity.

sections.title: A polynomial is not automatically an infinite expansion
sections.text: Taylor’s polynomial uses derivatives at one center. Taylor’s theorem supplies a finite remainder under sufficient differentiability; equality with the infinite Taylor series additionally requires that remainder to tend to zero. Smoothness alone does not ensure that.

sections.title: A smooth counterexample
sections.text: Define f(0)=0 and f(x)=exp(−1/x²) for x≠0. Every derivative at zero vanishes (exponential decay dominates each inverse power), so its Taylor series is zero, yet f(x)>0 away from zero. For eˣ on a bounded interval, by contrast, the factorial remainder bound tends to zero.

exercise.prompt: Approximate $e^{0.1}$ by $1+0.1+0.1^2/2$ and bound the error.
exercise.hint: Use a third-order remainder bounded by e^0.1(0.1)³/6; e^0.1<2 suffices.
exercise.solution: The estimate is 1.105. The error is less than 2·0.001/6=1/3000. This bound certifies the finite approximation.
rubric: Distinguish the polynomial from the exact value.
Bound the derivative over the interval.

sections.title: Coefficients and termination
sections.text: The coefficient of xⁿ in (1+x)^α is α(α−1)…(α−n+1)/n!, with constant term 1. For nonnegative integer α the series terminates as a polynomial. Otherwise its expansion is valid for |x|<1 and endpoints need separate analysis.

sections.title: A concrete expansion
sections.text: For α=1/2 the first terms are 1+x/2−x²/8+x³/16. This approximates √(1+x) near zero. For α=−1 the coefficients alternate and recover 1/(1+x)=1−x+x²−… inside the radius.

exercise.prompt: Find the quadratic Taylor approximation of $(1+x)^{-2}$ at zero.
exercise.hint: Use α=−2 in the coefficient formula.
exercise.solution: The first terms are 1−2x+3x², with remainder of order x³ near zero. The infinite nonterminating series has radius 1.
rubric: Divide the second falling product by 2!.
Do not treat the approximation as exact.

sections.title: Expand far enough to survive cancellation
sections.text: For (sin x−x)/x³, use sin x=x−x³/6+O(x⁵). After cancellation and division, the expression is −1/6+O(x²), so the limit is −1/6. Stopping at sin x≈x would discard the decisive term.

sections.title: Meaning of error symbols
sections.text: R(x)=O(xᵏ) means |R(x)|≤C|x|ᵏ in a sufficiently small neighborhood for some fixed C. R(x)=o(xᵏ) means its ratio to xᵏ tends to zero. Dividing an expansion by xᵐ also divides its error; retain enough orders to make the resulting error vanish.

exercise.hint: Keep the cubic term and a controlled higher-order remainder.
exercise.solution: Taylor gives numerator x³/6+O(x⁴), so the quotient is 1/6+O(x) and tends to 1/6.

sections.title: Separate points and displacements
sections.text: Points describe locations; their difference is a displacement vector. For A=(1,−1,2), B=(3,2,2), B−A=(2,3,0) has length √13. The dot product u·v=|u||v|cos θ measures alignment; normalization v/|v| requires v≠0.

sections.title: Projection is a signed component
sections.text: The scalar component of v along a unit vector e is v·e, and the vector projection is (v·e)e. Cauchy–Schwarz gives |u·v|≤|u||v|, the estimate later used for gradient bounds. Orthogonal vectors have dot product zero; the zero vector has no direction.

exercise.prompt: Project $v=(3,4,0)$ onto the direction $(1,1,0)$.
exercise.hint: Normalize the direction first.
exercise.solution: The unit direction is e=(1,1,0)/√2. The scalar component is 7/√2 and vector projection is (7/2,7/2,0). The residual (−1/2,1/2,0) is perpendicular to e.
rubric: Distinguish scalar component from vector projection.

sections.title: One trace, several clocks
sections.text: The circle r(t)=(cos t,sin t) traces once for 0≤t≤2π and twice for 0≤t≤4π. The image set is unchanged, but traversal-sensitive integrals count both passes. Reversing t reverses orientation; a positive increasing change of clock preserves it.

sections.title: Speed enters length
sections.text: For r(t)=(cos 2t,sin 2t), speed is 2. On [0,π] the length is $\int_0^\pi2\,dt$=2π, one traversal. The unit-speed parameter is arc length, not every parameter called t.

exercise.prompt: Compare the lengths of $r(t)=(\cos t,\sin t)$ on $[0,2\pi]$ and $[0,4\pi]$.
exercise.hint: Length integrates speed over the actual parameter interval.
exercise.solution: The lengths are 2π and 4π. The geometric image is the same circle, but the second curve traverses it twice.
rubric: Use the interval as part of the parametrized curve.
Do not confuse image length with traversal length.

sections.title: Use the defining constraint
sections.text: A line from A to B is A+t(B−A), 0≤t≤1. An ellipse x²/a²+y²/b²=1 is (a cos t,b sin t). For an intersection with z=x²+y², substitute a planar parametrization into z to satisfy both equations.

sections.title: Check coverage and orientation
sections.text: The intersection x²+y²=1 and z=x+y can be written (cos t,sin t,cos t+sin t), 0≤t≤2π. It traverses once counterclockwise in xy projection. Substitution verifies membership; the full parameter interval verifies coverage.

exercise.prompt: Parametrize the line segment from $(1,0,2)$ to $(0,3,1)$.
exercise.hint: Add t times the endpoint difference.
exercise.solution: r(t)=(1−t,3t,2−t), 0≤t≤1. At 0 and 1 it gives the assigned endpoints, with orientation from the first to the second.

sections.title: Regularity belongs to the parametrization
sections.text: A regular curve has nonzero velocity. The map r(t)=(t³,0) stops at zero but its image is a straight line, so a singular parameter need not mean singular geometry. The cusp (t²,t³) has zero velocity at zero and requires a separate local analysis.

sections.title: Length and reparametrization
sections.text: For a piecewise continuously differentiable curve, length is ∫|r′(t)|dt over its pieces. A regular change of parameter preserves length after the speed factor and bounds are transformed. Unit tangent r′/|r′| is defined only where speed is nonzero.

exercise.prompt: For $r(t)=(t,t^2)$, find speed and unit tangent at $t=1$.
exercise.hint: Differentiate components before taking the norm.
exercise.solution: r′(1)=(1,2), speed √5, and unit tangent (1,2)/√5. The tangent line is (1,1)+s(1,2).
rubric: Keep the selected point distinct from its velocity.

sections.title: Graph, level set, parametrization
sections.text: A graph z=f(x,y) has one height for each allowed planar input. A level set F(x,y,z)=c may fail to be a graph in a chosen direction. A sphere has two z values over most of its disk projection and needs upper/lower branches or surface charts.

sections.title: Read slices deliberately
sections.text: For z=x²−y², fixing y gives upward parabolas and fixing x gives downward parabolas. Level zero is the pair y=±x; positive and negative levels give differently oriented hyperbolas. Distinguish a horizontal contour from a vertical slice.

exercise.prompt: Why is $x^2+y^2+z^2=1$ not globally a graph $z=f(x,y)$?
exercise.hint: Inspect the two points above (0,0).
exercise.solution: Both (0,0,1) and (0,0,−1) lie on the sphere. A single-valued graph cannot assign both heights; separate hemisphere graphs are possible over appropriate domains.
rubric: Use an explicit repeated planar input.
Distinguish local representation from global representation.
exercise.solutionTex: (0,0,1),(0,0,-1)\in S\implies S\text{ is not a single }z\text{-graph}

sections.title: Open balls encode all directions
sections.text: A ball B(a,r) consists of points with distance less than r; its boundary sphere is excluded. A set is open when each member has some ball contained in it, and closed when it contains its limit points. A set can be neither open nor closed.

sections.title: Boundary depends on ambient space
sections.text: The disk x²+y²<1 is open in the plane, but the same disk embedded in ℝ³ has no three-dimensional interior. For limits on a restricted domain, only points belonging to that domain are admissible approaches.

exercise.prompt: Classify the annulus $1<\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\le 2$ as open, closed, or neither in $\mathbb R^2$.
exercise.hint: Test the included outer boundary and excluded inner boundary.
exercise.solution: It is neither: at an outer-circle point every ball leaves the set, while a sequence approaching the inner circle has a limit outside the set.
rubric: Name a missing limit point against closedness.

sections.title: One radius must cover every approach
sections.text: For a multivariable limit, every domain point with 0<|x−a|<δ must meet the output tolerance. A separate δ for each ray is insufficient unless one common positive radius works uniformly.

sections.title: Use norm inequalities
sections.text: For f(x,y)=2x−3y at zero, |2x−3y|≤√13√(x²+y²) by Cauchy–Schwarz. Choosing δ=ε/√13 proves the limit zero over every approach, including curved paths.

exercise.prompt: Prove $x^2+y^2$ tends to zero at the origin with an explicit $\delta$.
exercise.hint: Write the function in terms of the Euclidean radius r.
exercise.solution: The output is r². Given ε>0, choose δ=√ε; then 0<r<δ gives |f|<ε.
rubric: Use a radius independent of direction.

sections.title: Two paths can disprove
sections.text: For f(x,y)=xy/(x²+y²), the x-axis gives zero, while y=x gives 1/2 away from the origin. If a common limit existed, both admissible path restrictions would share it. Their difference proves nonexistence.

sections.title: Agreement cannot prove
sections.text: A finite or even infinite collection of selected paths can miss another obstruction. After path tests suggest a candidate, look for an estimate involving the full norm. The puncture and domain restrictions must hold along every path used.

exercise.prompt: For $x^2/(x^2+y^2)$, compare the two coordinate-axis limits at zero.
exercise.hint: Set y=0 and then x=0, excluding the origin.
exercise.solution: The x-axis gives 1 and the y-axis gives 0, so no limit exists.
rubric: Use two admissible paths approaching the same point.
State why distinct path limits contradict a common limit.

sections.title: Every line can agree
sections.text: For f(x,y)=x²y/(x⁴+y²), along y=mx with m≠0 the expression is mx/(x²+m²)→0; along y=0 it is zero, and the vertical axis is zero. Thus every line through the origin suggests zero.

sections.title: A curve reveals the obstruction
sections.text: Along y=x² the same expression is 1/2 for x≠0. The limit therefore fails. The denominator hints at the path: balance x⁴ with y² by choosing y proportional to x². Polar coordinates do not justify a limit unless the angular estimate is uniform.

exercise.prompt: What values occur along $y=kx^2$ for this function?
exercise.hint: Substitute and cancel x⁴ for x≠0.
exercise.solution: The value is k/(1+k²), independent of nonzero x. Different k give different path limits and exhibit the hidden family of obstructions.
rubric: Cancel only away from the puncture.

sections.title: Squeeze with the full radius
sections.text: For x²y/(x²+y²), use |y|≤r and x²/(x²+y²)≤1 to obtain |f|≤r. Defining the value zero at the origin makes it continuous. This uniform estimate handles all paths at once.

sections.title: Composition has a target condition
sections.text: If g tends to b and f is continuous at b through the relevant domain, then f∘g tends to f(b). Check that g’s nearby values lie in f’s domain; continuity of a formal expression outside its domain is not a usable theorem.

exercise.prompt: Does $xy/\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$, extended by zero, become continuous at zero?
exercise.hint: Use 2|xy|≤x²+y².
exercise.solution: Its absolute value is at most r/2 and therefore tends to zero. The extension is continuous.
rubric: Bound the absolute error by a quantity tending to zero.
Match the extension value to the limit.

sections.title: Every escape route counts
sections.text: A limit at infinity means for each ε>0 some R makes the output error smaller than ε whenever the input norm exceeds R within the domain. Either coordinate can diverge; one cannot test only x=y→∞.

sections.title: A uniform decay estimate
sections.text: For f(x,y)=1/(1+x²+y²), if r>R then f<1/(1+R²). Choosing R>1/√ε suffices to prove limit zero. The function x²/(x²+y²), by contrast, retains values 1 or 0 on the coordinate axes even arbitrarily far away.

exercise.prompt: Does $x/(1+x^2+y^2)$ tend to zero at infinity?
exercise.hint: Bound |x| by r.
exercise.solution: For r>0, its absolute value is at most r/(1+r²)≤1/r. Taking R>1/ε proves the limit zero.
rubric: Give a single R for every escape route.

sections.title: Hold the other input fixed
sections.text: For f(x,y)=x²y+sin y, fₓ=2xy and fᵧ=x²+cos y. The constant-held-fixed operation defines a coordinate slice derivative; it does not describe arbitrary combined input changes by itself.

sections.title: At a special point use the definition
sections.text: For a function defined by one formula away from zero and another at zero, differentiate the actual one-variable slice through zero. An off-origin derivative expression need not extend correctly by substitution at the missing point.

exercise.prompt: Find both partial derivatives of $f(x,y)=xe^y$ at $(2,0)$.
exercise.hint: In the x derivative eʸ is constant; in the y derivative x is constant.
exercise.solution: fₓ=eʸ gives 1 and fᵧ=xeʸ gives 2. These are the slopes of different coordinate slices at the same point.

sections.title: Cross product and rank
sections.text: For u,v in ℝ³, u×v is perpendicular to both and has magnitude equal to their parallelogram area. If the vectors are dependent the product is zero, so it supplies no normal direction. Swapping the order reverses the normal.

sections.title: Write a plane from its normal
sections.text: For point p and nonzero normal n, the plane is n·(x−p)=0. With u=(1,0,1), v=(0,1,1), u×v=(−1,−1,1). Through p=(0,0,2), the plane is z=x+y+2.

exercise.prompt: Find a normal and plane through the origin spanned by $(1,1,0)$ and $(0,1,1)$.
exercise.hint: Compute the ordered cross product.
exercise.solution: A normal is (1,−1,1), giving x−y+z=0. Its dot product with each spanning vector is zero.
rubric: Avoid confusing plane coefficients with a point on the plane.

sections.title: One linear map for all increments
sections.text: At a, differentiability means f(a+h)=f(a)+Lh+r(h) with r(h)/|h|→0. For scalar f with existing partials, the only candidate is Lh=∇f(a)·h. The candidate still needs an all-direction remainder check.

sections.title: Work a polynomial remainder
sections.text: For f(x,y)=x²+y² at (a,b), the exact increment is 2ah+2bk+h²+k². Dividing the remainder by √(h²+k²) gives √(h²+k²)→0, proving differentiability. The affine tangent plane includes the base value a²+b².

exercise.prompt: Find and justify the derivative of $f(x,y)=xy$ at $(a,b)$.
exercise.hint: Expand (a+h)(b+k) and bound |hk|.
exercise.solution: The linear map is L(h,k)=bh+ak. The remainder is hk, with |hk|/√(h²+k²)≤√(h²+k²)/2→0.
rubric: Identify a linear map, not just two numbers.

sections.title: Directional existence is weaker
sections.text: For g(x,y)=(x³−xy²)/(x²+y²), extended by zero, every directional derivative along v=(a,b) exists and equals (a³−ab²)/(a²+b²). This dependence on v is not linear, so it cannot be a total derivative.

sections.title: Test the only possible map
sections.text: Coordinate partials give L(x,y)=x. Along (t,t), g=0 while L=t, so |g−L|/√(2t²)=1/√2. The normalized error does not vanish. Yet |g|≤r, so g is continuous: continuity is another distinct property.

exercise.prompt: For this g, compare directional derivatives in $e_1$, $e_2$ and $e_1+e_2$.
exercise.hint: A linear derivative must preserve addition.
exercise.solution: They are 1, 0 and 0 respectively. Since 0≠1+0, the directional-derivative map is not additive, ruling out total differentiability.
rubric: Use directional vectors consistently without silently normalizing.

sections.title: A useful sufficient theorem
sections.text: If all first partial derivatives exist on a neighborhood and are continuous at a, then f is differentiable at a. This C¹ criterion is sufficient, not necessary. Partial derivatives existing only at a do not satisfy it.

sections.title: Finite versus asymptotic error
sections.text: If a twice continuously differentiable f has Hessian operator norm at most M along the segment from a to a+h, Taylor gives |f(a+h)−f(a)−∇f(a)·h|≤M|h|²/2. This finite bound needs an actual M; little-o alone does not provide one.

exercise.prompt: Bound the tangent-plane error for $f=x^2+y^2$ at any base point when $|h|\le 0.01$.
exercise.hint: The Hessian is twice the identity.
exercise.solution: M=2, so the error is at most |h|²≤0.0001. Here the remainder equals |h|² exactly.
rubric: Control the Hessian along the whole segment.
Distinguish a guaranteed bound from a sampled error.

sections.title: Do not hide cancellation
sections.text: For f(x,y)=x²+y² and r(t)=(cos t,sin t), the output is constant and its derivative zero. To see nonzero contributions, take r(t)=(t,t²): f(r(t))=t²+t⁴ and derivative 2t+4t³.

sections.title: Multiply derivative maps
sections.text: Along that path, ∇f(r(t))=(2t,2t²) and r′(t)=(1,2t), whose dot product is 2t+4t³. More generally D(f∘g)=Df(g)Dg, with matrix dimensions determined by the input and output spaces. Differentiability of both maps is a sufficient hypothesis.

exercise.prompt: For $f(x,y)=xe^y$ and $r(t)=(t,t^2)$, find $d(f\circ r)/dt$.
exercise.hint: Compute the two partial contributions separately.
exercise.solution: The derivative is e^(t²)·1 + t e^(t²)·2t = e^(t²)(1+2t²), agreeing with direct differentiation of t e^(t²).

sections.title: Which variable can be solved for?
sections.text: For a C¹ equation F(x,y,z)=0, if F_z(p)≠0 then a local C¹ graph z=g(x,y) exists near p. Its derivatives are gₓ=−Fₓ/F_z and gᵧ=−Fᵧ/F_z. This existence theorem is imported; differentiating a presumed graph alone does not prove its existence.

sections.title: Choose another chart when needed
sections.text: On the unit sphere at (0,0,1), F_z=2 and a local z graph exists. At (1,0,0), F_z=0 but F_x=2, so x can instead be expressed locally as a function of y,z. The surface remains smooth even though a chosen graph direction fails.

exercise.prompt: Find the tangent plane to $x^2+y^2+z^2=9$ at $(1,2,2)$.
exercise.hint: Use the nonzero gradient as normal.
exercise.solution: The gradient is (2,4,4). Thus 2(x−1)+4(y−2)+4(z−2)=0, or x+2y+2z=9.
rubric: Verify the point is on the surface.

sections.title: Normalize when measuring slope per distance
sections.text: For a differentiable scalar field, Dᵤf=∇f·u. A unit u measures change per unit distance; an arbitrary velocity v includes its speed. For f=x²+3y² at (1,1), the gradient is (2,6), so direction (1,1)/√2 gives slope 4√2.

sections.title: Existence of the gradient is not the whole hypothesis
sections.text: Coordinate partials define a vector when they exist, but the dot-product formula for all directions is guaranteed by total differentiability. At singular examples, compute the directional derivative from its limit rather than assuming the formula.

exercise.prompt: Find the directional derivative of $f=x^2+y^2$ at $(1,2)$ in direction $(3,4)$.
exercise.hint: Normalize (3,4) to length one.
exercise.solution: The gradient is (2,4), so the unit-direction derivative is (2,4)·(3/5,4/5)=22/5. Using velocity (3,4) instead would give 22 per unit time.
rubric: Declare whether the vector is a direction or a velocity.
Evaluate the gradient at the requested point.

sections.title: The maximum slope is a norm
sections.text: Cauchy–Schwarz gives ∇f·u≤|∇f| for unit u, with equality for u=∇f/|∇f| when ∇f≠0. At a stationary point all first-order slopes vanish, so the gradient picks no unique steepest direction.

sections.title: Contours and tangency
sections.text: If a differentiable curve lies in f=c, chain rule gives ∇f·r′=0. A nonzero gradient is normal to the level set. A zero gradient does not establish a smooth contour or a normal direction; inspect the geometry separately.

exercise.prompt: At $(1,1)$, find the steepest ascent direction for $f=x^2+2y^2$ and the maximum slope.
exercise.hint: Use gradient (2,4).
exercise.solution: Its norm is 2√5, and the unit direction is (1,2)/√5. The opposite direction gives steepest descent.
rubric: Distinguish maximum slope from the direction vector.

sections.title: Use the domain in the definition
sections.text: A local minimum compares values in some neighborhood intersected with the domain. Interior differentiable extrema require zero gradient; boundary extrema do not. A saddle has nearby values on both sides of the point’s value.

sections.title: Stationarity admits every outcome
sections.text: At the origin, x²+y² has a strict minimum, −x²−y² a strict maximum, and x²−y² a saddle. The zero function has non-strict maxima and minima everywhere. All have zero gradient at the origin.

exercise.prompt: Classify $f(x,y)=x^2-y^2$ at zero directly.
exercise.hint: Compare its coordinate axes.
exercise.solution: Along (t,0), f=t²>0; along (0,t), f=−t²<0 for nonzero t. Arbitrarily close values lie above and below f(0,0)=0, so the point is a saddle.
rubric: Do not identify a saddle from stationarity alone.

sections.title: Order and notation
sections.text: Here fₓᵧ means differentiate first in x and then in y. For f=x²y³, fₓᵧ=6xy²=fᵧₓ. State the convention because subscript and operator notation are sometimes read in different orders.

sections.title: When swapping is justified
sections.text: Continuity of the second partials on a neighborhood is a sufficient condition for equality of mixed partials. Merely existing at one point is insufficient. Higher-order cancellation identities likewise need appropriate smoothness rather than formal rearrangement alone.

exercise.prompt: Compute both mixed partials of $f=xe^y+y \sin x$.
exercise.hint: Differentiate in the stated order each time.
exercise.solution: fₓ=eʸ+y cos x, so fₓᵧ=eʸ+cos x. Also fᵧ=xeʸ+sin x, so fᵧₓ=eʸ+cos x. Smoothness justifies equality.

sections.title: Quadratic forms decide second-order shape
sections.text: For a C² scalar field at a stationary point, the quadratic Taylor term is hᵀHh/2. A positive-definite Hessian gives a strict minimum, a negative-definite one a strict maximum, and an indefinite one a saddle. In two dimensions, determinant positive plus fₓₓ positive/negative distinguishes the two definite cases.

sections.title: Mixed terms can rotate the shape
sections.text: For f=x²+4xy+y², H=[[2,4],[4,2]] has eigenvalues 6 and −2. Coordinate-axis slices both rise, yet along y=−x the value is −2x², so it is a saddle. A zero determinant is inconclusive; compare x⁴+y⁴ with x⁴−y⁴.

exercise.prompt: Classify $f=-2x^2-2xy-2y^2$ at zero.
exercise.hint: Compute the Hessian determinant and one diagonal entry.
exercise.solution: H=[[-4,−2],[−2,−4]], determinant 12>0 and fₓₓ<0, so it is negative definite and zero is a strict local maximum. Completing squares also shows global maximality.
rubric: State local classification and justify any global claim separately.

sections.title: Existence then candidate search
sections.text: A continuous function on a nonempty compact set attains maximum and minimum. Search interior stationary points, smooth boundary stationary points, corners, and singular locations. A local Hessian test does not compare all candidates.

sections.title: A disk example
sections.text: For f=x²+y²−2x on the closed unit disk, the unconstrained stationary point is (1,0), on the boundary. On the boundary f=1−2x, so its values range from −1 at (1,0) to 3 at (−1,0). Completing the square f=(x−1)²+y²−1 confirms the minimum.

exercise.prompt: Find extrema of $f=x+y$ on the square $[0,1]^2$.
exercise.hint: There are no interior stationary points; inspect the boundary and corners.
exercise.solution: The minimum is 0 at (0,0), maximum 2 at (1,1). Monotonicity in each coordinate proves these global bounds.
rubric: Explain attainment on the closed bounded set.

sections.title: Tangency is a necessary condition
sections.text: For a smooth constraint g=c with ∇g≠0, a constrained extremum has ∇f=λ∇g. Both gradients are normal to the same tangent directions. Solve the multiplier equations together with the original constraint.

sections.title: A singular constraint can hide candidates
sections.text: For g(x,y)=x³−y²=0 at zero, ∇g=0. The usual regular multiplier condition cannot be assumed there. Keep such feasible singular points as separate candidates instead of dividing by a gradient component.

exercise.prompt: Find the extrema of $x+y$ on $x^2+y^2=1$.
exercise.hint: The equations 1=2λx and 1=2λy force x=y.
exercise.solution: The candidates are (±1/√2,±1/√2) with matching signs, giving ±√2. Compactness ensures extrema, and Cauchy–Schwarz independently bounds |x+y|≤√2.
rubric: Compare all candidates and justify globality.

sections.title: One constraint leaves a tangent plane
sections.text: On a regular level surface in ℝ³, tangent vectors are perpendicular to ∇g. At a constrained extremum the derivative of f vanishes along that entire plane, making ∇f a multiple of ∇g.

sections.title: Linear objective on a sphere
sections.text: For f=x+2y+2z on the unit sphere, ∇f=(1,2,2) and ∇g=2(x,y,z). The candidates are ±(1,2,2)/3, giving values ±3. Norm comparison proves these are global extrema.

exercise.prompt: Maximize $2x-y+2z$ on $x^2+y^2+z^2=4$.
exercise.hint: Use Cauchy–Schwarz or solve the multiplier equations.
exercise.solution: The coefficient vector has norm 3 and the sphere radius is 2, so the maximum is 6 at (4/3,−2/3,4/3).
rubric: Scale the maximizing unit vector by the radius.
Check the point satisfies the constraint.

sections.title: Independence matters
sections.text: For two constraints g=c and h=d in ℝ³, independent gradients give a tangent direction ∇g×∇h. At a constrained extremum, ∇f lies in their span: ∇f=λ∇g+μ∇h. Dependent gradients invalidate this regular argument.

sections.title: Reduce when possible
sections.text: On x²+y²+z²=1 and z=0, maximizing x+y reduces to the unit circle in the xy-plane. The two gradients (2x,2y,0) and (0,0,1) are independent everywhere on the feasible circle, so the multiplier method is legitimate.

exercise.prompt: Find extrema of x on $x^2+y^2+z^2=1$ with $y=z$.
exercise.hint: Either use two multipliers or observe the feasible circle contains (±1,0,0).
exercise.solution: Since |x|≤1 on the sphere and both (±1,0,0) satisfy y=z, extrema are ±1 at those points. The constraint gradients are independent throughout the intersection.
rubric: Identify the regularity assumption when using multipliers.

sections.title: Cells contribute value times area
sections.text: Over a rectangle, a double Riemann sum adds f(sample)ΔxΔy. Both widths are essential. Integrability requires independence of increasingly fine tagged partitions; a single sampled mesh is a numerical approximation.

sections.title: Signed volume versus physical volume
sections.text: If f≥0, the integral is volume under its graph. If f takes both signs, it is signed accumulation. For f=x on [−1,1]×[0,1], the integral is zero while the volume between graph and plane is ∫|x|=1.

exercise.prompt: Compute the double integral of constant 3 over $[0,2]\times [0,4]$.
exercise.hint: Every cell contributes three times its area.
exercise.solution: The rectangle area is 8, so the integral is 24. With density units kg/m² and coordinates in metres, the result is kilograms.
rubric: Interpret the units of the integrand.

sections.title: A sufficient computational framework
sections.text: For a bounded region with a boundary of area zero and a function continuous on its closure, the double integral can be defined by extending the function by zero to a containing rectangle. The extension may jump at the region boundary but remains Riemann integrable under these sufficient assumptions.

sections.title: Name the stronger theorem
sections.text: The criterion that a bounded function on a rectangle is Riemann integrable when its discontinuity set has area zero is imported here. Lebesgue integration extends beyond Jordan regions and is an optional advanced framework, not a prerequisite silently hidden inside the elementary continuous-rectangle theorem.

exercise.prompt: Why can a continuous density on a disk be extended by zero for integration on a containing square?
exercise.hint: Where can new discontinuities occur?
exercise.solution: Only the circular boundary can acquire jumps. That boundary has area zero, so the bounded zero extension is Riemann integrable by the stated criterion. Its integral equals the disk integral.

sections.title: Order is a theorem, not typography
sections.text: A continuous function on a closed rectangle has equal double and iterated integrals. For zero extensions over ordinary piecewise smooth regions, a stronger integrability version is required because the extension may have boundary jumps.

sections.title: A sufficient extension for calculations
sections.text: For a bounded Riemann-integrable function whose slices are integrable apart from finitely many exceptional outer values, the iterated integrals agree with the double integral; changing bounded values on those exceptional slices does not affect it. In the Lebesgue setting, absolute integrability permits Fubini and nonnegativity permits Tonelli, but those are separate imported results.

exercise.prompt: Compute $\int_0^1\int_0^2(x+y)\,dy\,dx$ in both orders.
exercise.hint: The rectangle and continuous polynomial satisfy the elementary theorem.
exercise.solution: Integrating in y gives 2x+2, then total 3. Reversing gives $\int_0^2(1/2+y)\,dy$=3. The domain remains the same rectangle.
rubric: State why the swap is valid.
Keep each variable’s interval attached to it.

sections.title: Bounds describe a set
sections.text: The region 0≤x≤1, x²≤y≤x lies between a parabola and a line. For horizontal slices, 0≤y≤1 and y≤x≤√y. Derive these inequalities before changing the integration order.

sections.title: Split when one slice formula fails
sections.text: A region may need several Type I or Type II pieces. Splitting along an internal boundary does not duplicate area if pieces overlap only on boundaries of area zero. Draw or solve each boundary intersection and determine which curve actually limits a slice.

exercise.prompt: Reverse $\int_0^1\int_{x^2}^x f(x,y)\,dy\,dx$.
exercise.hint: Solve y≥x² and y≤x in the nonnegative quadrant.
exercise.solution: The reversed integral is $\int_0^1\int_y^{\sqrt y}f(x,y)\,dx\,dy$. The conditions give x≤√y and x≥y.

sections.title: Linearity concerns values
sections.text: For integrable f,g, ∫(af+bg)=a∫f+b∫g. It does not assert that ∫fg=(∫f)(∫g). A product separates only under additional structure, such as independent factors on a product rectangle.

sections.title: Additivity concerns regions
sections.text: If a region is split into pieces overlapping only on negligible boundaries, add their integrals. For signed accumulation, negative contributions remain negative. Overlapping pieces with positive area require subtracting the overlap to avoid double counting.

exercise.prompt: If $\iint_D f\,dA=2$ and $\iint_D g\,dA=-1$, find $\iint_D(3f-2g)\,dA$. Can you infer $\iint_D fg\,dA$?
exercise.hint: Apply linearity only to the linear combination.
exercise.solution: The first integral is 3·2−2·(−1)=8. The product integral cannot be determined from these two numbers alone.

sections.title: Derive the factor geometrically
sections.text: A polar cell has radial thickness dr and transverse length approximately r dθ, so area is approximately r dr dθ. The derivative columns of (r cos θ,r sin θ) have determinant r, confirming the local scale for r≥0.

sections.title: A coordinate singularity is not a hole
sections.text: At r=0 all angles describe one point and the determinant vanishes. For standard disk integrals this point has area zero and can be handled by a limiting argument. Angular endpoints also represent the same ray when using a full 2π interval.

exercise.prompt: Compute the area of the annular sector $1\le r\le 2$, $0\le \theta\le \pi/3$.
exercise.hint: Integrate the Jacobian r, not 1.
exercise.solution: The area is $\int_0^{\pi/3}\int_1^2r\,dr\,d\theta$=(π/3)(3/2)=π/2.
rubric: Distinguish parameter-rectangle area from physical area.

sections.title: Derive the shifted disk
sections.text: For (x−1)²+y²≤1, substitute polar coordinates to get r²−2r cos θ≤0. With r≥0 and r>0 this gives 0<r≤2cos θ, so cos θ≥0. Choose −π/2≤θ≤π/2, with r=0 included separately.

sections.title: Verify the area
sections.text: The integral is ∫ from −π/2 to π/2 of $\int_0^{2\cos\theta}r\,dr\,d\theta$=∫2cos²θ dθ=π. This matches a disk of radius one. A centered fixed-radius sector would represent a different region.

exercise.prompt: Write polar bounds for $(x-2)^2+y^2\le 4$.
exercise.hint: Repeat the algebra with center and radius 2.
exercise.solution: The bounds are −π/2≤θ≤π/2 and 0≤r≤4cos θ. The area is 4π, matching the disk radius 2.
rubric: Derive the angular range from nonnegative radius.
Handle the origin without dividing by zero.

sections.title: Volume cells need three widths
sections.text: A triple sum adds f(sample)ΔxΔyΔz. For f=1 it approximates volume; for mass density it approximates mass. A display containing only a few columns is a schematic, not a complete three-dimensional partition.

sections.title: Check a separable box
sections.text: For f=xyz on [0,1]×[0,2]×[0,3], continuity allows repeated integration and the product structure separates the result into (1/2)·2·(9/2)=9. This separation depends on both the factorized integrand and rectangular domain.

exercise.prompt: Integrate constant density 5 on a box with side lengths 2,3,4.
