exercise.hint: Multiply density by the volume.
exercise.solution: The integral is 5·2·3·4=120. If density is kg/m³, this is mass in kg.

sections.title: Project before setting height bounds
sections.text: The tetrahedron x,y,z≥0 with x+y+z≤1 projects onto x,y≥0, x+y≤1. Thus 0≤x≤1, 0≤y≤1−x, 0≤z≤1−x−y. The inner bounds depend only on outer variables.

sections.title: Each order describes the same solid
sections.text: A different outer coordinate requires a different projection. Writing all upper limits as 1 would replace the tetrahedron by a cube. Integrating 1 over the correct bounds gives volume 1/6.

exercise.prompt: Write bounds with x innermost for the same tetrahedron.
exercise.hint: Project onto the yz-plane.
exercise.solution: Use 0≤z≤1, 0≤y≤1−z, 0≤x≤1−y−z. Integrating 1 again yields 1/6.
rubric: Keep an inner bound free of its own integration variable.

sections.title: A planar polar map plus height
sections.text: Cylindrical coordinates are x=r cos θ, y=r sin θ, z=z with r≥0. The volume Jacobian is r. The angle is measured around the z-axis; it does not tilt toward that axis.

sections.title: Identify surfaces by equations
sections.text: r=2 is a cylinder, z=2 a horizontal plane, and z=r a cone above the plane. The z-axis has r=0 and nonunique θ; this coordinate singularity does not remove the axis from a solid.

exercise.prompt: Convert $x^2+y^2\le 4$ and $1\le z\le 3$ into cylindrical bounds.
exercise.hint: The planar projection is a full disk.
exercise.solution: 0≤r≤2, 0≤θ≤2π, 1≤z≤3, with volume element r dr dθ dz in a compatible chosen order.
rubric: Use the factor r for volume.

sections.title: Transform bounds and integrand
sections.text: Between z=r² and z=4, the surfaces meet at r=2. Volume is $\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^2\int_{r^2}^4 r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta$=8π. An integrand x²+y² becomes r², creating r³ after multiplication by the Jacobian.

sections.title: Do not count the Jacobian twice
sections.text: The measure r dr dθ dz already accounts for geometric stretching. If the physical density is itself r, the total factor r² has two different origins: density and volume measure. Label them separately.

exercise.prompt: Find the integral of $x^2+y^2$ over the cylinder of radius 1 and height 2.
exercise.hint: Use density r² and measure r.
exercise.solution: The result is $\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1\int_0^2r^3\,dz\,dr\,d\theta$=π.

sections.title: Fix the angle convention
sections.text: Use ρ≥0, azimuth θ around the z-axis, and polar angle φ down from the positive z-axis: x=ρ sin φ cos θ, y=ρ sin φ sin θ, z=ρ cos φ. Standard ranges are 0≤θ<2π and 0≤φ≤π.

sections.title: Distinguish coordinate singularities
sections.text: At ρ=0 every angle pair represents the origin. At φ=0 or π the azimuth is nonunique. These failures of coordinates do not imply the sphere or solid is geometrically singular.

exercise.prompt: What spherical coordinates describe $(0,0,-2)$?
exercise.hint: The point lies on the negative polar axis.
exercise.solution: ρ=2 and φ=π; any θ represents the same point. The nonunique azimuth is expected.
rubric: Allow nonunique coordinates on the axis.

sections.title: Three scale factors
sections.text: A small spherical cell has lengths approximately dρ, ρ dφ and ρ sin φ dθ. Its volume factor is ρ² sin φ. The signed determinant depends on coordinate order; scalar volume uses its absolute value.

sections.title: Cone and sphere bounds
sections.text: Inside a sphere of radius R and above the cone φ=π/4, use 0≤ρ≤R, 0≤φ≤π/4, 0≤θ≤2π. Volume is (2πR³/3)(1−1/√2), not a cylinder sector.

exercise.prompt: Integrate $x^2+y^2+z^2$ over the ball of radius R.
exercise.hint: The integrand is ρ² and the measure adds another ρ² sin φ.
exercise.solution: The integral is (R⁵/5)·2·2π=4πR⁵/5. For R=1 it is 4π/5.
rubric: Separate the integrand from the Jacobian.

sections.title: Columns are transformed edges
sections.text: For A=[[2,1],[0,3]], the unit square edges map to (2,0) and (1,3). Their parallelogram area is |det A|=6. Every cell has the same area scale because the map is linear.

sections.title: Orientation and collapse
sections.text: A negative determinant reverses orientation while keeping positive area scale. A zero determinant collapses the plane into a line or point, so a two-dimensional inverse does not exist. The determinant is a number; the derivative matrix is a different object.

exercise.prompt: Find signed and unsigned area factors for $T(u,v)=(u,-2v)$.
exercise.hint: Use the diagonal derivative matrix.
exercise.solution: The signed determinant is −2 and area scale is 2. The map reverses orientation.
rubric: Use absolute value for scalar area.

sections.title: A nonlinear map with variable scale
sections.text: Let T(u,v)=(u,(1+u)v), 0≤u,v≤1. Its derivative columns are (1,v) and (0,1+u), so det DT=1+u. The image is 0≤x≤1, 0≤y≤1+x: a trapezoid with area 3/2.

sections.title: Finite cells versus infinitesimal cells
sections.text: For [u,u+h]×[v,v+k], exact image area is hk(1+u+h/2). Dividing by hk gives finite scale 1+u+h/2, approaching the derivative factor 1+u as h→0. Location u and cell size h play different roles. The inverse v=y/(1+x) exists near this domain.

exercise.prompt: Compute $\iint_R y\,dA$ over that trapezoid using $T$.
exercise.hint: Replace y by (1+u)v and also include the Jacobian.
exercise.solution: The transformed integrand is (1+u)²v. Integrating v from 0 to 1 gives (1+u)²/2, and integrating u gives 7/6.
rubric: Transform the field as well as the measure.
Distinguish finite-cell scale from the derivative.

sections.title: Volume is a triple product
sections.text: For T(u,v,w), the signed determinant of its three derivative columns measures oriented volume scale. Scalar volume uses its absolute value. Swapping two parameter columns reverses the sign without changing the physical volume.

sections.title: Order in spherical coordinates
sections.text: With columns ordered (ρ,φ,θ) for x=ρ sin φ cos θ, y=ρ sin φ sin θ, z=ρ cos φ, the determinant is ρ²sin φ. The order (ρ,θ,φ) has its negative. Both give the same positive volume factor on the standard interior range.

exercise.prompt: Find the volume scale for $T(u,v,w)=(2u,-3v,4w)$.
exercise.hint: Multiply the diagonal entries.
exercise.solution: The signed determinant is −24 and the volume scale is 24. The negative sign records orientation reversal.

sections.title: State the map’s scope
sections.text: A sufficient change-of-variables setting is a one-to-one C¹ map on a neighborhood of a region with nonzero determinant, plus an integrable transformed field and ordinary negligible boundaries. The transformed integral uses f(T(u))|det DT(u)|.

sections.title: Local invertibility is not global injectivity
sections.text: The map (u,v)↦(eᵘcos v,eᵘsin v) has nonzero determinant e^(2u), but repeats whenever v increases by 2π. Integrating over two full angle turns counts the image twice. Restrict the parameter range or explicitly account for multiplicity.

exercise.prompt: Why does a polar integral over $\theta\in [0,4\pi]$ double-count a disk?
exercise.hint: Compare points at θ and θ+2π.
exercise.solution: They have identical physical coordinates for each positive r, so almost every disk point is covered twice. Using the usual r Jacobian over that interval computes twice the disk integral.
rubric: Check global coverage, not only the determinant.
Explain multiplicity away from negligible seams.

sections.title: Invert at corresponding points
sections.text: For an invertible differentiable map S=T⁻¹, DS(T(u))DT(u)=I. Thus det DS(T(u))=1/det DT(u). The locations matter: reciprocal determinants are evaluated at points related by the map.

sections.title: A nonlinear example
sections.text: For u=x and v=y/(1+x), with x>−1, the forward determinant is 1/(1+x). The inverse is x=u,y=(1+u)v and its determinant is 1+u. When integrating in u,v, use the latter absolute factor.

exercise.prompt: For $u=2x$ and $v=3y$, what factor converts $du dv$ to $dx dy$?
exercise.hint: Compute the inverse map, or reciprocate the nonzero determinant.
exercise.solution: The inverse is x=u/2,y=v/3, so dx dy=(1/6)du dv.
rubric: Do not insert the forward determinant 6.

sections.title: Density accumulates with length
sections.text: For a parametrized curve r(t), ∫_C f ds=∫f(r(t))|r′(t)|dt. Reversing orientation preserves the value because speed is nonnegative. Repeated traversal repeats the accumulation.

sections.title: Non-unit speed is visible
sections.text: For r(t)=(2cos t,2sin t), speed is 2. With density f=3, one traversal has integral $\int_0^{2\pi}6\,dt$=12π. Using dt alone would underestimate by a factor of two.

exercise.prompt: Integrate density $f(x,y)=x$ along $r(t)=(t,2t)$, $0\le t\le 1$.
exercise.hint: The speed is constant √5.
exercise.solution: The integral is √5$\int_0^1t\,dt$=√5/2. Reversing the traversal leaves the scalar line integral unchanged.

sections.title: Components depend on position
sections.text: A vector field F assigns a vector to each point of its domain. For F=(−y,x), arrows are tangential to circles about zero; for F=(x,y), arrows are radial. Arrow normalization improves legibility but hides magnitude unless a scale or readout supplies it.

sections.title: Domain is part of the field
sections.text: The field (−y/(x²+y²),x/(x²+y²)) excludes the origin. A plot that omits one arrow does not repair the missing domain point; theorem hypotheses must respect that puncture.

exercise.prompt: At $(1,0)$, compare radial $F=(x,y)$ and rotational $G=(-y,x)$.
exercise.hint: Substitute the point into each component.
exercise.solution: F=(1,0) points outward and G=(0,1) is tangent counterclockwise. Their dot product is zero.
rubric: Evaluate the field at the point.
Distinguish field vector from position vector when they differ.

sections.title: Work uses a signed component
sections.text: Work is ∫F(r(t))·r′(t)dt. Parallel force and velocity contribute positively, opposed ones negatively, and perpendicular components contribute zero. Unlike a scalar length integral, reversing traversal reverses the sign.

sections.title: A transverse component contributes nothing
sections.text: On r(t)=(t,0), 0≤t≤1, F=(1,5) has dot product 1 with r′=(1,0). Work is 1 despite the large vertical force component. For F=(−1,5), work is −1.

exercise.prompt: Find the work of $F=(2,3)$ along the segment from $(0,0)$ to $(1,2)$.
exercise.hint: Use r(t)=(t,2t).
exercise.solution: The dot product (2,3)·(1,2)=8 is constant, so work is 8. The reverse path gives −8.
rubric: Use velocity rather than unit tangent alone.

sections.title: Three differentials are one dot product
sections.text: The expression P dx+Q dy+R dz becomes [P(r)x′+Q(r)y′+R(r)z′]dt. Each differential follows the same parameter interval; none is an independent integration variable.

sections.title: Check terms individually
sections.text: Along r(t)=(t,t²), 0≤t≤1, ∫y dx+x dy becomes ∫(t²+2t²)dt=1. The form is d(xy), so endpoints independently give 1−0=1.

exercise.prompt: Evaluate $\oint(x\,dy-y\,dx)$ around the unit circle counterclockwise.
exercise.hint: Use x=cos t, y=sin t and differentiate both.
exercise.solution: The integrand becomes cos²t+sin²t=1, giving 2π over [0,2π]. Reversing orientation gives −2π.
rubric: Carry the minus sign in dx.

sections.title: Each piece gets its own parameter
sections.text: For a path from A to B to C, parametrize both oriented segments and add their integrals. Shared endpoints contribute no interval length. Reversing a piece changes its vector line integral sign but not a scalar length integral.

sections.title: Compare different paths
sections.text: For F=(y,0), from (0,0) to (1,1), traveling horizontally then vertically gives work 0. Traveling vertically then horizontally gives work 1. The same endpoints do not imply the same work without conservativeness.

exercise.prompt: Compute $\int y\,dx$ along $(0,0)\to(1,0)\to(1,1)$.
exercise.hint: On the first segment y=0; on the second dx=0.
exercise.solution: Both pieces contribute zero, so the integral is zero. The alternative path through (0,1) gives 1.
rubric: Respect the order and direction of pieces.

sections.title: Circulation is work on a closed traversal
sections.text: For F=(−y,x) and the unit circle counterclockwise, F(r)=r′ and the dot product is 1, giving circulation 2π. For the radial field (x,y), it is zero because field and velocity are perpendicular.

sections.title: A field can change the sign around a path
sections.text: For constant F=(1,0) on a circle, local work density is −sin t. Some arcs contribute positively and others negatively, with total zero. Zero net work does not mean every local contribution vanishes.

exercise.prompt: Find circulation of $F=(-2y,2x)$ around a radius-R circle counterclockwise.
exercise.hint: Both field and velocity scale with R.
exercise.solution: The dot product is 2R², giving circulation 4πR². Clockwise traversal changes the sign.

sections.title: Apply chain rule along the curve
sections.text: If F=∇φ on a domain containing the entire piecewise smooth path, then F(r)·r′=(φ∘r)′. Integrating gives φ(end)−φ(start). A closed path then has zero work.

sections.title: Construct a potential with a missing function
sections.text: For F=(2xy,x²+2y), integrate the first component in x to get φ=x²y+C(y). Differentiating in y and matching the second component gives C′=2y, hence φ=x²y+y²+constant.

exercise.prompt: Find work of that field from $(0,0)$ to $(1,2)$.
exercise.hint: Evaluate the potential at endpoints.
exercise.solution: φ(1,2)=2+4=6 and φ(0,0)=0, so work is 6 along every admissible path in ℝ².
rubric: Verify both partials of the potential.

sections.title: Curl-free needs a domain theorem
sections.text: A C¹ field on a simply connected open domain with zero curl is conservative. On an arbitrary domain, zero curl is only a local condition. A potential always forces zero curl when mixed derivatives may be interchanged.

sections.title: The punctured-plane counterexample
sections.text: F=(−y/r²,x/r²) has zero scalar curl away from zero, yet its circulation around the unit circle is 2π. The loop surrounds an excluded point, so no global single-valued potential exists on the punctured plane. On a suitable cut domain an angle potential is possible.

exercise.prompt: Can Green’s theorem on the full disk justify zero circulation for this vortex?
exercise.hint: Is the field defined on a neighborhood of the whole disk?
exercise.solution: No. It is undefined at the center, violating the theorem’s domain hypothesis. Direct circulation is 2π; an annulus would have both outer and inner boundaries.
rubric: Check the interior as well as the curve.
Account for an inner boundary when using an annulus.

sections.title: Orient the whole boundary
sections.text: For a positively oriented simple closed piecewise smooth curve bounding a suitable planar region, with P,Q continuously differentiable on a neighborhood, ∮P dx+Q dy=∫∫(Qₓ−Pᵧ)dA. Positive orientation keeps the region on the left; inner boundaries of holes therefore run clockwise.

sections.title: Why internal edges disappear
sections.text: Partitioning a region into smaller pieces gives two traversals of every shared edge with opposite directions. Their line integrals cancel, leaving the outer and hole boundaries. This motivates the theorem; a full proof requires controlling the partition and regularity.

exercise.prompt: Find $\oint(-y\,dx+x\,dy)$ around the unit circle counterclockwise using Green.
exercise.hint: Compute Qₓ−Pᵧ.
exercise.solution: The scalar curl is 1−(−1)=2. The disk area is π, so circulation is 2π.
rubric: Check the field on the entire disk.

sections.title: Choose a field whose curl is one
sections.text: The forms x dy, −y dx, and (x dy−y dx)/2 all integrate to area on a positively oriented simple boundary because each corresponding scalar curl equals 1. Reverse orientation and the signed result changes sign.

sections.title: A polygon reduces to endpoint data
sections.text: On a straight edge from (xᵢ,yᵢ) to (xⱼ,yⱼ), the symmetric form contributes (xᵢyⱼ−xⱼyᵢ)/2. Summing edges gives the shoelace formula. Self-intersecting traversals produce signed multiplicity-weighted area rather than automatically the union’s geometric area.

exercise.prompt: Use boundary data to find the area of triangle $(0,0)$, $(3,0)$, $(0,2)$ in that order.
exercise.hint: Sum the three cross-products and divide by two.
exercise.solution: Only the edge (3,0)→(0,2) contributes 6 before halving. The area is 3 and the ordering is counterclockwise.

sections.title: Two parameters trace a surface
sections.text: A chart r(u,v) maps a planar parameter region into space. Regularity requires rᵤ×rᵥ≠0. To integrate without multiplicity, also check coverage: a regular map can cover the same physical patch more than once.

sections.title: Seams are coordinate artifacts
sections.text: A sphere chart r(φ,θ)=(sin φ cos θ,sin φ sin θ,cos φ) repeats at the angular seam and degenerates at the poles. Multiple charts or exclusion of negligible boundary sets can handle these defects; they do not make the sphere itself nonsmooth.

exercise.prompt: Parametrize the cylinder $x^2+y^2=4$ for $0\le z\le 3$.
exercise.hint: Use angle and height as independent parameters.
exercise.solution: r(θ,z)=(2cos θ,2sin θ,z), 0≤θ≤2π,0≤z≤3. It covers the side once apart from the repeated seam.
rubric: Explain seam duplication and distinguish the cylinder caps.

sections.title: Differentiate one parameter at a time
sections.text: For r(u,v)=(u,v,u²+v²), the tangent vectors are rᵤ=(1,0,2u) and rᵥ=(0,1,2v). Their cross product is (−2u,−2v,1), a nonzero upward normal.

sections.title: Tangent plane versus the curved patch
sections.text: At (u,v)=(1,1), the surface point is (1,1,2) and normal (−2,−2,1), yielding z=2x+2y−2. The plane is the affine first-order approximation, not the whole surface.

exercise.prompt: Find tangent vectors and a normal for $r(u,v)=(u,v,uv)$ at $(1,2)$.
exercise.hint: Evaluate derivatives at the parameter pair, not at the 3D point.
exercise.solution: rᵤ=(1,0,2), rᵥ=(0,1,1), and rᵤ×rᵥ=(−2,−1,1). The surface point is (1,2,2).
rubric: Distinguish parameter pair from physical point.
Verify the normal is perpendicular to both tangents.

sections.title: A local parallelogram supplies area
sections.text: The parameter cell du dv maps approximately to edges rᵤdu and rᵥdv, giving dS=|rᵤ×rᵥ|du dv. The norm removes orientation but retains stretch; using a unit normal here would lose the area factor.

sections.title: Graphs are a special case
sections.text: For z=f(x,y), r=(x,y,f) gives dS=√(1+fₓ²+fᵧ²)dx dy. On the plane z=x+2y over a unit square, the factor is √6 and the area is √6.

exercise.prompt: Find the area of $z=3x$ over $0\le x\le 2$, $0\le y\le 1$.
exercise.hint: The graph area factor is constant.
exercise.solution: The factor is √(1+9)=√10. Multiplying by projected area 2 gives 2√10.
rubric: Use surface area rather than projected area.
Keep the factor under the square root.

sections.title: Density times area
sections.text: The scalar surface integral is ∫∫f(r(u,v))|rᵤ×rᵥ|du dv. It is unaffected by reversing orientation, although repeating coverage repeats the integral.

sections.title: A plane with variable density
sections.text: On z=x+y over the unit square, density f=z becomes u+v and area factor √3. The integral is √3$\int_0^1\int_0^1(u+v)\,du\,dv$=√3. Using only the projected measure would miss the slope factor.

exercise.prompt: Integrate constant density 2 over a sphere of radius R.
exercise.hint: Multiply density by surface area.
exercise.solution: The result is 8πR². It does not change if inward rather than outward orientation is named, because this is a scalar area integral.

sections.title: Orientation is a continuous choice
sections.text: An orientation chooses one of the two unit normal directions continuously across a regular surface. Reversing parameter order reverses rᵤ×rᵥ. A closed bounding surface usually uses outward normals; open surfaces need an explicit convention.

sections.title: A Möbius strip has no global side
sections.text: Following a local normal around a Möbius strip returns it reversed. Thus one global continuous normal cannot be chosen. Local charts and scalar area still make sense; a globally oriented flux or ordinary oriented Stokes surface requires more care.

exercise.prompt: For the graph $z=x^2+y^2$, which cross-product sign gives downward orientation?
exercise.hint: The standard (x,y) order produces a positive z component.
exercise.solution: The upward area vector is (−2x,−2y,1)dx dy. Downward uses its negative, (2x,2y,−1)dx dy.
rubric: Choose sign from the requested direction.
Do not discard the area magnitude when integrating flux.

sections.title: Flux retains the normal sign
sections.text: Flux is ∫∫F·n dS, or ∫∫F(r)·(rᵤ×rᵥ)du dv with a compatible parameter orientation. The dot product measures only the normal component; reversing the normal reverses flux.

sections.title: Oblique fields and cancellation
sections.text: For constant F=(1,0,0) on an outward unit sphere, local flux is positive on the right hemisphere and negative on the left, giving total zero. This differs from the radial field F=(x,y,z), which is outward everywhere and has flux 4π.

exercise.prompt: Find upward flux of $F=(1,2,3)$ through the unit square in $z=0$.
exercise.hint: The upward unit normal is (0,0,1).
exercise.solution: The dot product is 3, so flux is 3. Horizontal components contribute zero. Downward orientation gives −3.

sections.title: Curl measures oriented circulation density
sections.text: In three dimensions curl F has components (Rᵧ−Q_z,P_z−Rₓ,Qₓ−Pᵧ). Its dot product with a chosen unit normal measures infinitesimal circulation per area in that plane, under smoothness hypotheses.

sections.title: Curved arrows alone are misleading
sections.text: The field (−y,x,0) has curl (0,0,2), while (−y/r²,x/r²,0) has zero curl away from the z-axis despite circular arrows. The latter has an excluded singular axis, so its global circulation behavior needs the domain.

exercise.prompt: Find curl of $F=(0,0,xy)$.
exercise.hint: Only derivatives of the third component are nonzero.
exercise.solution: Curl F=(x,−y,0). At (1,2,0) it is (1,−2,0), describing oriented circulation in corresponding coordinate planes.
rubric: Distinguish curl from the field itself.

sections.title: Divergence is a signed scalar
sections.text: For F=(P,Q,R), divergence is Pₓ+Qᵧ+R_z. Positive divergence means local net outward flux density, not necessarily arrows pointing directly away from the origin.

sections.title: A non-radial example
sections.text: For F=(x,−y,0), divergence is zero: expansion in the x direction balances contraction in y. For F=(x,y,z), divergence is 3. Arrow length and direction alone do not supply the derivative balance.

exercise.prompt: Compute divergence of $F=(x^2,yz,z^2)$. Where is it zero?
exercise.hint: Differentiate each component in its matching coordinate.
exercise.solution: Divergence is 2x+z+2z=2x+3z, zero on the plane 2x+3z=0.
rubric: Do not add the components without differentiating.

sections.title: Write the cancellations
sections.text: For a C² scalar φ, curl(∇φ)=0 because each component is a difference of equal mixed partials. For a C² vector field, div(curl F)=0 by the same pairwise cancellations.

sections.title: Converse statements need separate conditions
sections.text: Curl-free does not always mean a global gradient on a punctured domain. Divergence-free does not automatically provide a globally defined vector potential on every domain. These identities are necessary structural checks, not universal converse theorems.

exercise.prompt: Could $F=(x,y,z)$ be the curl of a $C^2$ vector field on an open ball?
exercise.hint: Compute its divergence.
exercise.solution: No: div F=3, whereas the divergence of the curl of a C² field must be zero.
rubric: Use the identity as a necessary condition.

sections.title: Boundary and normal are paired
sections.text: Stokes relates ∮∂S F·dr to ∫∫S(curl F)·n dS for a suitable oriented piecewise smooth surface and C¹ field on a neighborhood. Viewed along the chosen positive normal, the positive boundary runs counterclockwise. Across glued patches, shared edges cancel.

sections.title: Choose the easier surface lawfully
sections.text: For F=(−y/2,x/2,0), curl is (0,0,1). Around a unit horizontal circle counterclockwise, the flat disk gives flux π. Another admissible spanning surface with the same induced boundary has the same curl flux, provided the field remains smooth near it.

exercise.prompt: Find circulation of $F=(-y,x,0)$ around the unit circle viewed clockwise from above.
exercise.hint: Use a downward-oriented disk.
exercise.solution: Curl F=(0,0,2). With downward normal, flux is −2 times the disk area, giving −2π.
rubric: Match the boundary to the surface normal.
Check the field on a neighborhood of the spanning surface.

sections.title: The surface must close the region
sections.text: For a suitable bounded solid V with outward-oriented boundary and C¹ field near its closure, total flux equals ∫∫∫V div F dV. An open cap or side surface needs its missing pieces included and then subtracted.

sections.title: Singularities and holes
sections.text: The field r/|r|³ is singular at zero, so the theorem cannot be applied to a ball containing zero despite vanishing divergence away from it. On a shell the inner boundary points toward the center as an outward normal from the shell, and its flux cancels the outer contribution.

exercise.prompt: Find outward flux of $F=(x,y,z)$ through a sphere of radius R.
exercise.hint: Use divergence 3 and the enclosed volume.
exercise.solution: The flux is 3·(4πR³/3)=4πR³. Directly, F·n=R and surface area is 4πR², giving the same answer.
rubric: Use outward orientation on a closed surface.
Check with the direct area calculation.

sections.title: Four fully specified practice problems
sections.text: These are self-contained replacements preserving the review’s methods and results, not a transcription of missing source statements. (1) Compute outward curl flux for F=(y,−x,z) on the cone z=√(x²+y²), 0≤z≤1, joined to the cylinder x²+y²=1,1≤z≤4. (2) Compute upward curl flux for F=(x+y²,y+z²,z+x²) on the first-octant triangle x+y+z=3. (3) Compute clockwise circulation of F=(0,xy) on the triangle (0,0),(0,12),(3,0). (4) For φ=x²y+$\int_0^xe^{-s^2}\,ds$+sin(πy²/2)/π, compute ∫∇φ·dr on r(t)=(0,1−t),0≤t≤1.

sections.title: Strategy and independent checks
sections.text: For (1), the top boundary is clockwise under the outward side orientation; r=(cos t,−sin t,4) gives integrand 1 and answer 2π. Excluding a tiny cone-tip cap and taking its limit handles the apex. For (2), curl=(−2z,−2x,−2y); its dot product with (1,1,1) is −6, so flux is −27. For (3), Qₓ−Pᵧ=y and clockwise orientation gives −72. For (4), endpoint potential gives φ(0,0)−φ(0,1)=−1/π. The field is (2xy+e^(−x²),x²+y cos(πy²/2)).

exercise.prompt: For problem (3), reverse the triangle direction and compute the new circulation by both Green and a boundary parametrization.
exercise.hint: Only the diagonal edge contributes for the field (0,xy).
exercise.solution: Counterclockwise circulation is 72. On the diagonal from (3,0) to (0,12), use x=3−3t,y=12t: Qdy=(3−3t)(12t)12dt, whose integral is 72; the other edges contribute zero.
rubric: Specify the field and all path data.

sections.title: Map every boundary
sections.text: For the first-quadrant region bounded by y=x³,y=2x³,xy=1,xy=3, take u=y/x³ and v=xy. The new rectangle is 1≤u≤2,1≤v≤3. The inverse x=(v/u)^(1/4), y=u^(1/4)v^(3/4) maps its four edges to the actual curved boundaries.

sections.title: Check sign, scale, and bounds
sections.text: The inverse determinant is −1/(4u), so scalar area uses 1/(4u). Integrating gives (ln2)/2. Since the factor lies between 1/8 and 1/4 on a rectangle of area 2, the result must lie between 1/4 and 1/2; this catches a mistaken forward determinant.

exercise.prompt: Compute $\iint_D xy\,dA$ over the same region.
exercise.hint: The integrand xy becomes v.
exercise.solution: The integral is $\int_1^2\int_1^3\frac{v}{4u}\,dv\,du$=(ln2)/4·4=ln2.

sections.title: Why the box is centered
sections.text: For an axis-aligned box whose eight vertices lie on 2x²+72y²+18z²=288, compare vertices differing in only one coordinate. Their squared endpoints must agree, so a nondegenerate box has opposite coordinate pairs. Its positive half-lengths x,y,z give volume 8xyz.

sections.title: Global bound without multipliers
sections.text: Set X=x/12,Y=y/2,Z=z/4. The constraint becomes X²+Y²+Z²=1. AM–GM gives X²Y²Z²≤1/27, so XYZ≤1/(3√3). Since 8xyz=768XYZ, maximum volume is 256/√3, attained at X=Y=Z=1/√3. Boundary boxes have zero volume.

exercise.prompt: For an ellipsoid $x^2/a^2+y^2/b^2+z^2/c^2=1$ with $a,b,c>0$, find the largest axis-aligned inscribed box.
exercise.hint: Normalize coordinates and maximize the product.
exercise.solution: The half-lengths are a/√3,b/√3,c/√3, so volume is 8abc/(3√3). Positivity and AM–GM establish the global maximum, while degenerate boundary volumes vanish.
rubric: Prove a global bound and its equality case.

sections.title: Enumerate rather than sample
sections.text: For f=x⁴−2x²+y³−3y, stationarity gives x∈{−1,0,1} and y∈{−1,1}, producing six points. The Hessian is diagonal with entries 12x²−4 and 6y, so its signs classify every candidate.

sections.title: Keep all values and types
sections.text: At (±1,1), both entries are positive: strict local minima of value −3. At (0,−1), both are negative: strict local maximum of value 2. At (±1,−1) the signs differ: saddles of value 1; (0,1) is a saddle of value −2. The cubic y term makes the full surface unbounded in both directions, so none is a global extremum.

exercise.prompt: At $(0,1)$, show directly that the value $-2$ is neither a local minimum nor a local maximum.
exercise.hint: Compare small displacements along x and along y.
exercise.solution: Along (h,1), f+2=h⁴−2h²<0 for small nonzero h. Along (0,1+k), f+2=3k²+k³>0 for small nonzero k. Both signs occur arbitrarily close.
rubric: Keep the base value in the comparison.

sections.title: A successful all-direction estimate
sections.text: For f=(x⁴+y⁴)/r away from zero and f(0)=0, both coordinate partials are zero. Since x⁴+y⁴≤r⁴, |f|/r≤r²→0. Thus the derivative is the zero map, with δ=√ε supplying an explicit normalized-error guarantee.

sections.title: A continuous failure
sections.text: For g=(x³−xy²)/(x²+y²) with g(0)=0, the candidate derivative is L(x,y)=x. The remainder is −2xy²/(x²+y²). Along (t,t), its normalized magnitude is 1/√2, so differentiability fails. Nevertheless |g|≤r proves continuity. A graph of a canonical bowl cannot establish either result.

exercise.prompt: Explain why testing just the two coordinate axes would wrongly suggest differentiability of g.
exercise.hint: Evaluate g−L on each axis.
exercise.solution: On both coordinate axes the remainder is zero, so those tests see no error. Along the diagonal the normalized error stays 1/√2. Total differentiability needs one estimate for all small vectors, not only coordinate directions.
rubric: Identify the unique candidate map from the partials.
